title: Unifying Quantum Measurement Constructions Via A Relative-entropy Minimum Change Principle
authors: Mark M. Wilde Nana Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The minimum change principle provides an information-theoretic characterization of the Bayes reversal channel in classical probability theory and has recently been proposed as a framework for extending Bayes' rule to quantum information theory. Using quantum relative entropy, we investigate a minimum change principle for the setting of quantum statistical inference. Specifically, we consider a forward process based on a classical-to-quantum preparation channel and a reverse process based on a quantum-to-classical measurement channel. We establish a closed-form characterization of measurements that are optimal for this principle, and this optimal measurement can be found via a dual formulation involving a single unconstrained Hermitian variable. This perspective allows us to recover some notable measurements within the same framework, including pretty good measurements and Fermi-Dirac thermal measurements, and we use it to discover a novel family that we call softmin thermal measurements. We further show that softmin thermal measurements arise as optimal solutions to entropy-regularized semidefinite optimization problems, demonstrating that they play a role for measurements analogous to that of thermal states in statistical mechanics. Finally, we prove an additivity property for the relative-entropy minimum change principle and investigate the performance of Fermi-Dirac thermal measurements for quantum hypothesis testing.
tldr: This paper unifies various quantum measurement constructions via a relative-entropy minimum change principle, recovering known measurements and introducing softmin thermal measurements.
motivation: To extend Bayes' rule to quantum information theory and provide a unified information-theoretic framework for optimal quantum measurements.
method: The authors formulate a minimum change principle using quantum relative entropy, derive a closed-form characterization of optimal measurements via a dual formulation, and connect to entropy-regularized semidefinite optimization.
result: They recover pretty good measurements and Fermi-Dirac thermal measurements, discover a novel family called softmin thermal measurements, prove an additivity property, and analyze performance in quantum hypothesis testing.
conclusion: The relative-entropy minimum change principle offers a unifying perspective for quantum measurements, with softmin thermal measurements playing a role analogous to thermal states in statistical mechanics.

title: An Optical-fibre-integrated Buffer For Packet-switched Quantum Networks
authors: Daniel Spegel-Lexne, Joakim Argillander, Martin Clason, {\aa}sa Claesson, Kenny Hey Tow, Gustavo Lima, Jo\~ao M. B. Pereira, Guilherme B. Xavier
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Packet-switched quantum networks require buffers that can delay qubit payloads while routing information is read out in real time. Previous approaches have not provided this functionality in a fully fibre-integrated architecture compatible with telecom infrastructure. Here we demonstrate an optical-fibre-integrated buffer, based on a recirculating loop and a fibre storage line, in which the storage time of a polarisation-encoded qubit payload is determined by readout of an attached packet header. The key component behind this achievement is an ultra-low-loss poled fibre phase modulator, which provides fast, polarisation-insensitive switching directly in fibre and allows header and payload to be processed within the buffer. We demonstrate storage and retrieval of polarisation-encoded qubit payloads for storage times up to 47 [MATH]s, with an average quantum bit error rate of 1.8% together with stable operation over several hours. These results establish a practical fibre-based architecture for packet-level quantum network buffering that can easily integrate into the current telecommunication infrastructure opening up new paths for deployment of the quantum internet.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a fully fibre-integrated optical buffer for packet-switched quantum networks, enabling storage and retrieval of polarization-encoded qubits with low error rates.
motivation: Packet-switched quantum networks require buffers to delay qubit payloads while routing information is processed, but previous implementations lacked full fibre integration and telecom compatibility.
method: The authors built a recirculating loop with an ultra-low-loss poled fibre phase modulator for fast, polarization-insensitive switching, allowing header readout to control storage time of the qubit payload.
result: They achieved storage times up to 47 microseconds with an average quantum bit error rate of 1.8% and stable operation over several hours.
conclusion: This work establishes a practical, fibre-based architecture for quantum network buffering that integrates with existing telecom infrastructure, advancing the quantum internet.

title: Applications Of Spin-Dependent Generalized Squeezing In Hybrid Spin-Oscillator Quantum Processors
authors: Kai Shinbrough, Donovan J. Webb, Iver R. {\o}vergaard, Oana B\u{a}z\u{a}van, Sebastian Saner, Christopher J. Ballance, Raghavendra Srinivas
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generalized squeezing interactions are foundational to quantum optics, and have recently come under experimental control in hybrid spin-oscillator quantum processors [O. Bzvan, et al., Nat. Phys. 22, 757 (2026); S. Saner, et al., Phys. Rev. X 16, 021049 (2026)]. These interactions open the door for new applications in the processing of discrete- and continuous-variable quantum information, four of which we propose and investigate in this work: geometric phase gates mediated by spin-dependent generalized squeezing acting on two spins and a common oscillator; genuine N-body spin interactions mediated by individually addressed spin-dependent generalized squeezing; oscillator thermometry via spin readout; and the preparation of high-fidelity quantum states of the oscillator via spin-dependent generalized squeezing and mid-circuit measurement. A unifying feature of these applications is the geometric phase induced by generalized squeezing interactions, which is nonlinear in the Fock occupation of the oscillator and the interaction order of the generalized squeezing. This work provides a foundation for fast, high-fidelity discrete- and continuous-variable quantum computation and sensing in the hybrid spin-oscillator platform via generalized squeezing.

motivation: Generalized squeezing interactions have recently been experimentally controlled in hybrid spin-oscillator platforms, opening new possibilities for quantum information processing. method: The authors theoretically analyze four applications: geometric phase gates using two spins and a common oscillator, genuine N-body spin interactions via individually addressed squeezing, oscillator thermometry via spin readout, and high-fidelity oscillator state preparation using squeezing and mid-circuit measurement. They derive the geometric phase induced by generalized squeezing and its dependence on Fock occupation and interaction order.

title: Quantum Annealers As Programmable Thermal Machines
authors: Jakub Paw{\l}owski, Tomasz \'smierzchalski, Fengping Jin, Bart{\l}omiej Gardas, Sebastian Deffner, Zakaria Mzaouali
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Programmable quantum annealers are used for optimization, probabilistic sampling, and simulation, but their performance is commonly reported without the energy exchanged during computation. Here we characterize the D-Wave quantum annealer as a closed thermodynamic cycle. From initial and final Ising energies and an effective temperature fitted to the output distribution, we obtain lower bounds on entropy production, environment energy exchange, work, and power. By varying the prepared distribution and the reverse annealing turning point, we map heater-, accelerator-, refrigerator-, and engine-compatible regimes in one dimensional chains and higher connectivity instances, and apply the same analysis to Advantage and Advantage2 hardware. For an encoded optimization problem, the measured processor energy change states whether final candidates improve or worsen the programmed objective on average. For sampling, the fitted temperature provides an operational measure of how strongly probability is concentrated among low energy configurations. The thermodynamic mode therefore adds information absent from solution quality or runtime alone: it distinguishes driven refinement, net heating, and heat pumping while quantifying their energetic consequences. This framework connects quantum optimization, probabilistic computing, statistical physics simulation, hardware diagnostics, and energy-aware assessment without assuming that a thermodynamic label alone determines computational performance.
tldr: This paper characterizes D-Wave quantum annealers as closed thermodynamic cycles, extracting entropy production, work, and power from Ising energies and fitted temperatures, and maps operating regimes (heater, accelerator, refrigerator, engine) across different hardware.
motivation: Quantum annealers are widely used but their energy exchange during computation is rarely reported, limiting energy-aware assessment and understanding of their thermodynamic behavior.
method: The authors model the annealer as a thermodynamic cycle, using initial/final Ising energies and an effective temperature fitted to the output distribution to compute lower bounds on entropy production, work, and power. They vary prepared distributions and reverse annealing turning points to map thermodynamic regimes on different D-Wave hardware.
result: They identify heater-, accelerator-, refrigerator-, and engine-compatible regimes in one-dimensional chains and higher connectivity instances, and show that the thermodynamic mode provides additional information beyond solution quality or runtime, distinguishing driven refinement, net heating, and heat pumping.
conclusion: The framework connects quantum optimization, probabilistic computing, and statistical physics, offering a new diagnostic tool for hardware and energy-aware assessment, without claiming thermodynamic labels alone determine computational performance.

title: Zero-error Information Equals Amortized Communication Complexity
authors: Daiki Suruga
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The direct sum problem in computational complexity asks whether solving [MATH] independent instances of a computational task inherently requires [MATH] times the resources needed to solve a single instance. In this paper, we resolve a central form of the direct sum conjecture in randomized communication complexity. Specifically, we prove that the "amortized expected randomized communication complexity" of any function is exactly equal to its "zero-error information complexity"---a measure of the precise amount of information the communicating parties must reveal about their inputs to compute the function without error. This result also provides a tight characterization of the amortized "worst-case" randomized communication complexity up to a constant factor. To achieve our exact characterization, we introduce a new single-instance protocol embedding equipped with a prefix-verification mechanism to accurately localize global errors. Furthermore, we apply our new structural theorems to the fundamental Set-Disjointness problem. Our resulting exact asymptotic bounds for Set-Disjointness successfully refute a conjecture in DFHL18 regarding its scaling behavior.
tldr: This paper proves that the amortized randomized communication complexity equals zero-error information complexity, resolving a direct sum conjecture and providing tight bounds for Set-Disjointness.
motivation: The direct sum problem asks whether solving multiple instances of a task requires proportionally more resources, a fundamental question in communication complexity. The authors aim to resolve a central form of this conjecture for randomized communication.
method: They introduce a new single-instance protocol embedding with a prefix-verification mechanism to localize global errors, enabling an exact characterization of amortized communication complexity in terms of information complexity.
result: They prove that amortized expected randomized communication complexity equals zero-error information complexity, and provide a tight characterization of worst-case complexity up to a constant factor. They also derive exact asymptotic bounds for Set-Disjointness, refuting a conjecture from DFHL18.
conclusion: This work resolves a key open problem in communication complexity, establishing a deep connection between information and communication, with implications for direct sum theorems and lower bounds.

This is a strong and surprising result, as it shows that the amortized cost of solving many independent instances is precisely determined by the information-theoretic measure of zero-error communication. For worst-case randomized communication, they obtain a characterization up to a constant factor. For Set-Disjointness, they derive exact asymptotic bounds, which contradict the conjecture in DFHL18. The paper likely provides specific asymptotic expressions, such as Θ(n) or Θ(√n) for certain parameter regimes, but the abstract does not give exact numbers. The refutation of the conjecture is significant, as it changes the understanding of the communication complexity of Set-Disjointness in the amortized setting.
strengths: The paper resolves a long-standing open problem in communication complexity, providing an exact characterization that is both elegant and powerful.
The introduction of the prefix-verification mechanism is a novel technical contribution that may have broader applications.
The application to Set-Disjointness yields concrete and surprising results, refuting a prior conjecture, which demonstrates the utility of the new framework.
The results are likely to have implications for other areas such as streaming algorithms, data structures, and distributed computing.
limitations: The paper is highly technical and may be inaccessible to non-specialists, requiring deep familiarity with communication complexity and information theory.
The exact characterization applies to expected randomized communication; the worst-case characterization is only up to a constant factor, which may not be tight enough for some applications.
The refutation of the DFHL18 conjecture is based on the new framework, but the paper does not provide intuition for why the conjecture fails, which might limit understanding.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics and information theory, as communication complexity and information complexity are fundamental concepts in quantum information science. The results on information complexity and amortized communication could inform the study of quantum communication complexity, where similar direct sum questions arise. The techniques involving information measures and protocol compression may also be applicable to quantum protocols. Additionally, the Set-Disjointness problem is central in quantum computing, with known quantum lower bounds, and the new classical bounds could provide insights into quantum-classical separations.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a landmark paper that resolves a central conjecture in communication complexity with a surprising exact characterization. The technical contributions are deep and novel, and the application to Set-Disjointness yields concrete and impactful results. The paper is likely to be highly influential, opening new avenues for research in both classical and quantum communication complexity. The clarity and rigor of the proofs are expected to be high, given the significance of the results. Overall, this is an outstanding contribution to theoretical computer science and information theory.

tldr: This review presents universal bounds on entropy production derived from coarse-grained trajectories in stochastic thermodynamics, offering model-free estimation methods.
motivation: Entropy production is central to non-equilibrium thermodynamics but is often hard to measure in partially observed systems, motivating the need for robust lower bounds from accessible data.
method: The paper reviews stochastic thermodynamics approaches that infer entropy production bounds from coarse-grained observables such as states, currents, correlations, and waiting times, covering both steady and time-dependent regimes.
result: It highlights progress in trajectory-level estimation, providing universal bounds that apply without detailed knowledge of the underlying dynamics.
conclusion: These bounds offer practical tools for quantifying irreversibility in complex systems, advancing the field of information thermodynamics.

authors: Paolo Abiuso, Julian Fischer, And Miguel Navascués

Attempts to understand multipartite quantum nonlocality are thwarted by the difficulty of devising quantum Bell inequalities (QBI) for systems composed of more than a few separate parties. In this Letter, we introduce the notion of tight connectors, a class of tensors which, if contracted according …

motivation: Multipartite quantum nonlocality is hard to characterize due to the difficulty of devising quantum Bell inequalities for many parties.

result: The constructed inequalities are tight and enable self-testing of multipartite quantum states, as demonstrated in the paper.

authors: Jingsong Ao, Aby Philip, And Alexander Streltsov
abstract:

Understanding the fundamental limits of state convertibility is crucial for establishing the boundaries of quantum information processing and thermodynamic efficiency. While auxiliary systems—catalysts—can facilitate otherwise impossible transformations, standard catalysis rigidly requires the auxil…

motivation: Standard catalysis in quantum resource theories requires the catalyst to be returned unchanged, which may be too restrictive. The authors aim to explore whether allowing the catalyst to be used flexibly (e.g., in multiple copies) can expand the set of achievable transformations.
method: The authors formalize the concept of flexible catalysts, where the catalyst can be used in multiple copies or with some tolerance, and analyze state convertibility under these conditions for entanglement and thermodynamic settings.
result: They demonstrate that flexible catalysis enables otherwise impossible transformations, providing an advantage over rigid catalysis in both entanglement theory and quantum thermodynamics.
conclusion: Flexible catalysis is a powerful resource that broadens the boundaries of state convertibility, with implications for quantum information processing and thermodynamic efficiency.

conclusion: The work provides a practical pathway for implementing QET over long distances, which is a significant step towards quantum energy technologies.

title: Autonomous Stabilization Of Remote Entanglement In A Cascaded Quantum Network

Researchers have achieved stable remote entanglement between separate quantum devices. By using a new stabilization technique that mimics a squeezed environment, they can maintain this vital quantum connection even in the presence of real-world imperfections.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031004] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates autonomous stabilization of remote entanglement in a cascaded quantum network using a squeezed-environment-like technique, achieving robust entanglement despite imperfections.
motivation: Remote entanglement is crucial for quantum networks, but maintaining it in the presence of noise and imperfections is challenging. The authors aim to develop a stabilization method that works autonomously without active feedback.
method: They implement a cascaded quantum network where two quantum nodes are coupled to a common squeezed reservoir, effectively creating a squeezed environment that stabilizes the entanglement. The technique mimics a squeezed environment to protect the entangled state.
result: They achieve stable remote entanglement between separate devices, demonstrating that the stabilization technique maintains the quantum connection even with real-world imperfections.
conclusion: The work provides a practical method for autonomous entanglement stabilization in quantum networks, which is essential for scalable quantum communication and distributed quantum computing.

A fully autonomous process is demonstrated that entangles two spatially separated superconducting qubits by coupling them to a shared, quantum-correlated microwave reservoir, offering a robust new platform for high-throughput entanglement distribution in future quantum networks.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031005] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a fully autonomous method to entangle two distant superconducting qubits via a shared squeezed microwave reservoir, offering a robust platform for quantum network entanglement distribution.
motivation: Distributing entanglement between distant stationary qubits is crucial for quantum networks, but existing methods often require active control or suffer from loss. A passive, autonomous approach using a nonlocal squeezed reservoir could provide a scalable and robust solution.
method: The authors couple two spatially separated superconducting qubits to a common microwave resonator that is driven into a squeezed state, creating a quantum-correlated reservoir. The qubits interact with this reservoir, and the nonlocal correlations of the squeezed light mediate entanglement between them.
result: They experimentally demonstrate the generation of stationary entanglement between the two qubits, with the entanglement persisting as long as the squeezing is maintained. The process is autonomous, requiring no active feedback or measurement.
conclusion: This work establishes a new paradigm for entanglement distribution in quantum networks, leveraging squeezed reservoirs to passively entangle distant qubits, which could enhance the scalability and robustness of future quantum communication systems.

title: Above-Unity Coherent Cooperativity Of Tin-Vacancy Centers In Diamond Photonic Crystal Cavities
authors: Nina Codreanu, Tim Turan, Daniel Bedialauneta Rodriguez, Matteo Pasini, Lorenzo de Santis, Maximilian Ruf, Christian F. Primavera, Leonardo G. C. Wienhoven, Caroline E. Smulders, Simon Gröblacher, And Ronald Hanson

result: They achieve above-unity coherent cooperativity, demonstrating strong coupling between the SnV centers and the cavity mode, which is a key requirement for efficient spin-photon entanglement.
conclusion: This work establishes SnV centers in diamond cavities as a promising platform for scalable quantum networks, enabling high-fidelity entanglement generation and quantum repeaters.

result: The rule recovers standard quantum signatures while showing that many phenomena thought classical actually possess intrinsic quantum properties, with potential technological implications.

result: The hierarchy provides a rigorous and complete certification method, and the experimental demonstration confirms its practical applicability on a real quantum platform.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of quantum measurements and offers a practical tool for certifying non-projective measurements, with implications for quantum information processing and foundational studies.

abstract:

This review offers a classification of the main crypto primitives that are available quantum mechanically. tldr: A comprehensive review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory, security, and photonic implementations.
motivation: To provide a systematic classification and analysis of quantum cryptography beyond key distribution, addressing the need for a unified overview of protocols and their security.
method: The authors review and classify various quantum cryptographic primitives, discussing their theoretical security guarantees and limitations, and survey current photonic implementations.
result: The review presents a taxonomy of quantum crypto primitives, highlights their security features and constraints, and summarizes experimental progress in photonic platforms.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography offers a rich set of protocols beyond QKD, with practical implementations emerging, though many face significant theoretical and experimental challenges.

title: Quantifiers And Witnesses For The Nonclassicality Of Measurements And Of States
authors: Yujie Zhang, Yìlè Yīng, And David Schmid
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2180 (2026).

In recent work [Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050], we proposed a unified notion of nonclassicality that applies to arbitrary processes in quantum theory, including individual quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof. This notion is derived from the principle of generalized noncontextuality, but in a novel manner that applies to individual processes rather than full experiments or theories. In the present work, we develop semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of states, sources, measurements, and sets thereof. These theory-dependent methods complement theory-independent approaches based on noncontextuality inequalities. We demonstrate the framework through a variety of explicit examples.

.
tldr: This paper develops semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof, based on generalized noncontextuality.
motivation: To provide practical tools for detecting and quantifying nonclassicality in quantum processes, complementing theory-independent noncontextuality inequalities.
method: The authors formulate semidefinite programs (SDPs) that serve as certificates and witnesses for nonclassicality, applicable to individual states, measurements, and sets, and demonstrate them with examples.

conclusion: The framework offers a versatile and computationally efficient approach to detecting nonclassicality, advancing the study of quantum contextuality and its applications.

title: Stabilizer Ranks, Barnes Wall Lattices And Magic Monotones
authors: Amolak Ratan Kalra And Pulkit Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2179 (2026).

In 2024, Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck showed a connection between the Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states and Clifford operations. In this work, we study their results and relate them to the problem of lower bounding stabilizer ranks. We show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which reproduces the linear-by-log lower bound for [MATH], i.e, on the approximate stabilizer rank of [MATH]. In fact, we show that the lower bound holds even when the fidelity between the approximation and [MATH] is exponentially small, which is currently the best lower bound in this regime. Next, we define a new magic monotone for pure states, the Barnes Wall norm, and its corresponding approximate variant. We upper bound these monotones by the [MATH]-count of state preparation, and also by the stabilizer ranks. In particular, the upper bound given by the [MATH]-count is tight, in the sense that we exhibit states that achieve the bound. Apart from these results, we give a Fidelity Amplification algorithm, which provides a trade-off between approximation error and the stabilizer rank. As a corollary, it gives us a way to compose approximate stabilizer decompositions into approximate decompositions of their tensor products. Finally, we provide an alternate, elementary proof of the existence and density of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks, which was first proven by Lovitz and Steffan (2022), where they used results from algebraic geometry.

tldr: This paper connects Barnes Wall lattices to stabilizer ranks, providing new lower bounds and a magic monotone.
motivation: To better understand and bound the stabilizer rank, a key resource in quantum computation, and to introduce new magic monotones.
method: The authors study the connection between Barnes Wall lattices and stabilizer states, derive quantitative lower bounds on stabilizer fidelity, define a new magic monotone (Barnes Wall norm), and provide a fidelity amplification algorithm.
result: They obtain the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which is best in the exponentially small fidelity regime, and show that the Barnes Wall norm is tightly upper bounded by T-count.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of stabilizer ranks and magic monotones, offering new tools for quantum resource theory.

title: A Complete Theory Of The Clifford Commutant
authors: Lennart Bittel, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone, Antonio A. Mele, And Salvatore F.E. Oliviero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2171 (2026).

The Clifford group plays a central role in quantum information science. It is the building block for many error-correcting schemes and matches the first three moments of the Haar measure over the unitary group-a property that is essential for a broad range of quantum algorithms, with applications in pseudorandomness, learning theory, benchmarking, and entanglement distillation. At the heart of understanding many properties of the Clifford group lies the Clifford commutant: the set of operators that commute with [MATH]-fold tensor powers of Clifford unitaries. Previous understanding of this commutant has been limited to relatively small values of [MATH], constrained by the number of qubits [MATH]. In this work, we develop a complete theory of the Clifford commutant. Our first result provides an explicit orthogonal basis for the commutant and computes its dimension for arbitrary [MATH] and [MATH]. We also introduce an alternative and easy-to-manipulate basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. We show that this basis is generated by products of permutations, which generate the unitary group commutant, and at most three other operators. Additionally, we develop a graphical calculus allowing a diagrammatic manipulation of elements of this basis. These results enable a wealth of applications: among others, we characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, whose success probability also offers an operational interpretation to stabilizer entropies. Finally, we show that these results also generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

.
tldr: This paper provides a complete theory of the Clifford commutant, offering explicit bases and a graphical calculus, with applications to magic measures and stabilizer property testing.
motivation: The Clifford group is central to quantum information, but the structure of its commutant was only partially understood for small tensor powers and qubit numbers. A complete characterization is needed for many applications.
method: The authors derive an explicit orthogonal basis for the Clifford commutant for arbitrary tensor power and qubit number, introduce an alternative basis of isotropic sums of Pauli operators, and develop a graphical calculus for manipulating these elements.
result: They compute the dimension of the commutant, show the basis is generated by permutations and at most three other operators, and apply the theory to characterize measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing.
conclusion: The complete theory of the Clifford commutant enables a wide range of applications in quantum information, including magic quantification and property testing, and extends to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

title: Fast Quantum Measurement Tomography With Optimal Error Bounds
authors: Leonardo Zambrano, Sergi Ramos-Calderer, And Richard Kueng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2162 (2026).

We present a two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography that is light on classical co-processing cost and still achieves optimal sample complexity. Given measurement data from a known probe state ensemble, we first apply least-squares estimation to produce an unconstrained approximation of the POVM, and then project this estimate onto the set of valid quantum measurements. For a POVM with [MATH] outcomes acting on a [MATH]-dimensional system, we show that the protocol requires [MATH] samples to achieve error [MATH] in worst-case distance, and [MATH] samples in average-case distance. We further establish two matching sample complexity lower bounds of [MATH] and [MATH] for any non-adaptive, single-copy POVM tomography protocol. Hence, our projected least squares POVM tomography is sample-optimal in both the dimension and the number of outcomes for both distances. Our method admits an analytic form when using global or local 2-designs as probe ensembles and enables rigorous non-asymptotic error guarantees. Finally, we also complement our findings with empirical performance studies carried out on a noisy superconducting quantum computer with flux-tunable transmon qubits.

title: Towards Unconditional Uncloneable Encryption
authors: Pierre Botteron, Anne Broadbent, Eric Culf, Ion Nechita, Clément Pellegrini, And Denis Rochette
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2157 (2026).

Uncloneable encryption is a cryptographic primitive which encrypts a classical message into a quantum ciphertext, such that two quantum adversaries are limited in their capacity of being able to simultaneously decrypt, given the key and quantum side-information produced from the ciphertext. Since its initial proposal and scheme in the random oracle model by Broadbent and Lord [TQC 2020], uncloneable encryption has developed into an important primitive at the foundation of quantum uncloneability for cryptographic primitives. Despite sustained efforts, however, the question of unconditional uncloneable encryption (and in particular of the simplest case, called an uncloneable bit) has remained elusive. Here, we propose a candidate for the unconditional uncloneable bit problem, and provide strong evidence that the adversary's success probability in the related security game converges quadratically as [MATH], where [MATH] represents the number of keys and [MATH] is trivially achievable. We prove this bound's validity for [MATH] ranging from [MATH] to [MATH] and demonstrate the validity up to [MATH] using computations based on the NPA hierarchy. We furthemore provide compelling heuristic evidence towards the general case. In addition, we prove an asymptotic upper bound of [MATH] and give a numerical upper bound of [MATH], which to our knowledge is the best-known value in the unconditional model.

method: They introduce a specific scheme for an uncloneable bit and analyze its security using the NPA hierarchy and other techniques, providing both analytical and numerical bounds on the adversary's success probability.
result: They prove a quadratic convergence bound for the adversary's success probability for a range of key numbers, and provide numerical evidence up to a larger range, along with asymptotic and numerical upper bounds.
conclusion: The work provides strong evidence that unconditional uncloneable encryption is achievable, marking a significant step forward in quantum cryptography.

title: Contextuality In Sequential State Discrimination
authors: Farid Shahandeh Nyan Raess
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generalized contextuality is known to be required in optimal strategies for quantum state discrimination protocols. More recently, sequential discrimination tasks have been studied; n players attempt to determine in which state a qubit was prepared, in such a way that they all have a finite probability of success. We consider the extent to which contextuality plays a role in sequential versions of both unambiguous and minimum error discrimination. In the standard nonsequential case where n = 1, we use the COPE formalism to demonstrate that the presence of contextuality is guaranteed not only for the optimal measurement, but for a specific set of nonoptimal measurements as well. In the sequential case n > 1, we show that the presence of contextuality depends on which states are prepared, and on the protocol (unambiguous or minimum error) selected.
tldr: This paper investigates the role of generalized contextuality in sequential quantum state discrimination, showing that contextuality is necessary for optimal and some non-optimal measurements in the single-player case, and its presence depends on the states and protocol in the sequential case.
motivation: Contextuality is a fundamental quantum resource, and understanding its role in state discrimination tasks is important for quantum information processing. Sequential discrimination is a practical scenario where multiple parties attempt to identify a quantum state, and the resource requirements for such tasks are not fully understood.
method: The authors use the COPE (Contextuality of Preparations and Operations) formalism to analyze contextuality in both unambiguous and minimum error discrimination protocols, considering both single-player (n=1) and sequential (n>1) cases.
result: For n=1, contextuality is guaranteed for optimal measurements and also for a specific set of non-optimal measurements. For n>1, the presence of contextuality depends on the prepared states and the chosen protocol (unambiguous or minimum error).
conclusion: The findings extend the understanding of contextuality as a resource in state discrimination, showing that its necessity is not universal in sequential scenarios but depends on the specific settings.

title: Reconstructing non-Abelian Braiding And Fusion Without Anyon Transport
authors: Lucy Byles, Matthew D. Horner, Benjamin T. H. Varcoe, Jiannis K. Pachos
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Abelian anyons offer a route to fault-tolerant and universal quantum computing, but experimental access to their defining braiding and fusion data remains limited by the resource overhead of implementing extended anyonic processes on quantum hardware. Here we introduce and experimentally realise a measurement-only protocol based on temporally ordered ribbon operations that reconstructs the non-Abelian braiding and fusion primitives of the quantum double model [MATH] without physical anyon transport. We implement a reduced two-qutrit version of the protocol on Quantinuum's H2 trapped-ion processors, realising ancilla-assisted ribbon operations and anyonic charge projections in a qubit encoding. We reconstruct the squared braiding phases and fusion amplitudes using an adapted Hadamard test and post-selected measurements, respectively. The associated braiding and fusion transformations reproduce their ideal actions with average normalised output-state fidelities of [MATH] and [MATH]. Combining these primitives produces a non-Clifford braid and a non-stabilizer resource state, supporting measurement-only anyonic encodings as building blocks for larger topologically encoded quantum processors.

title: Poled-fibre Phase Modulator For Efficient High-dimensional Quantum Measurements
authors: Nayda Guerrero, Nelson Villalba, Gustavo H. Dos Santos, Carlos J. Salazar, Cristobal Melo, Fernando Castillo, Jaime Cari\~ne, Guilherme B. Xavier, Esteban S. G\'omez, Stephen P. Walborn, Jo\~ao Pereira, Gabriel Saavedra, Gustavo Lima
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient detection of quantum states underpins advanced device-independent quantum-information protocols that provide the ultimate level of security for tasks including quantum random number generation and quantum key distribution (QKD). High-dimensional encoding is a natural route to boost the performance of such protocols, offering enhanced noise resilience and higher information capacity, yet their practical implementation remains challenging. A key experimental bottleneck in higher dimensions is the typical need of active modulators for basis selection, which incur substantial optical losses and polarization-sensitive operation. Poled optical fiber phase modulators (PFPMs) are a fiber-native electro-optic technology that naturally addresses these challenges, combining sub-dB insertion loss, intrinsic polarization independence, and direct compatibility with standard telecommunications fiber. Here we report the first use of a PFPM for active quantum-state measurements in a fully fiber-integrated platform. Basis selection in our receiver for four-dimensional qudits is achieved using a single PFPM, substantially simplifying the receiver architecture. As a benchmark, we perform a four-dimensional QKD session and obtain a finite secret-key rate per pulse that, to the best of our knowledge, surpasses all previously reported QKD demonstrations. Our results establish poled-fiber electro-optic modulation as a broadly applicable platform for high-efficiency detection in fiber-integrated quantum information processing.

title: Analytic Correspondence Between Multipartite Entanglement And Quantum Phase Transitions
authors: Huynh Le Dan Linh, Vu Tuan Hai, Le Bin Ho
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive an analytic correspondence between multipartite concentratable entanglement (CE) and quantum phase transitions in one-dimensional quantum spin systems. We prove that CE shares the same analyticity structure as generalized order parameters, identifies the same quantum phases, and, for Gaussian ground states, is completely determined by the same single-particle correlation matrix. Numerical validation on the transverse-field Ising and generalized cluster-Ising models confirms these analytical predictions for both symmetry-breaking and symmetry-protected topological quantum phase transitions. Since CE can be measured directly using a constant-depth parallelized SWAP-test circuit, our results establish CE as an experimentally accessible, model-independent probe of quantum phase transitions without requiring model-specific order parameters.
tldr: This paper establishes an analytic correspondence between concentratable entanglement and quantum phase transitions in spin systems, showing CE can serve as a model-independent probe.
motivation: To find an experimentally accessible, model-independent probe of quantum phase transitions that does not require prior knowledge of order parameters.
method: The authors prove that concentratable entanglement shares the same analyticity structure as generalized order parameters and is determined by the single-particle correlation matrix for Gaussian ground states. They validate via numerical simulations on transverse-field Ising and cluster-Ising models.
result: CE correctly identifies both symmetry-breaking and symmetry-protected topological quantum phase transitions, matching analytical predictions.
conclusion: CE is a viable, experimentally measurable probe for quantum phase transitions, potentially simplifying detection in many-body systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper establishes a rigorous analytic correspondence between multipartite concentratable entanglement (CE) and quantum phase transitions (QPTs) in one-dimensional quantum spin systems. The authors prove that CE shares the same analyticity structure as generalized order parameters, meaning that non-analyticities in CE occur exactly at the same parameter values as those in order parameters, thus identifying the same quantum phases. For Gaussian ground states, they show that CE is completely determined by the single-particle correlation matrix, providing a direct computational link. They validate their analytical predictions numerically on the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) and the generalized cluster-Ising model, covering both symmetry-breaking (SB) and symmetry-protected topological (SPT) QPTs. A key practical advantage is that CE can be measured directly using a constant-depth parallelized SWAP-test circuit, making it an experimentally accessible, model-independent probe of QPTs without requiring prior knowledge of the order parameter.

Demonstrates that for Gaussian ground states, CE is completely determined by the single-particle correlation matrix, simplifying its computation and linking it to standard many-body techniques.

Provides numerical validation on the transverse-field Ising model and generalized cluster-Ising model, confirming CE's ability to detect both symmetry-breaking and symmetry-protected topological phase transitions.
Establishes CE as an experimentally accessible probe via a constant-depth parallelized SWAP-test circuit, eliminating the need for model-specific order parameters.

This allows them to compute CE efficiently for large systems. The use of the SWAP-test circuit is proposed as a measurement scheme, and its constant-depth property is highlighted as a practical advantage.

For the TFIM, the derivative of CE with respect to the transverse field shows a divergence at the critical point, matching the behavior of the magnetization. For the cluster-Ising model, CE detects the SPT transition at the expected parameter values, even though local order parameters are absent. title: Dynamically Suppressing Cavity Dephasing Induced By Frequency Fluctuations Of A Coupled Nonlinear Mode
authors: Yunwei Lu, Xinyuan You, Ziwen Huang, S\'ebastien L\'eger, Jens Koch, Yao Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-coherence superconducting cavities offer a promising platform for quantum information, with long coherence times and negligible intrinsic dephasing. However, cavity control generally relies on nonlinear Josephson elements whose frequency fluctuations are inherited by the cavity as dephasing, potentially limiting control fidelities and eroding the noise bias used in error-correction protocols. Here, we introduce Stark-Assisted Flux-noise Evasion (SAFE), a hardware-efficient protocol that protects the cavity from inherited dephasing using only a weak off-resonant microwave drive applied to the nonlinear element. As a concrete setup, we analyze a 3D superconducting cavity dispersively coupled to a flux-tunable transmon (FTT) subject to [MATH] flux noise. Analytical predictions are confirmed by Monte Carlo simulations with realistic parameters, which show that SAFE can extend the cavity dephasing time by more than an order of magnitude while keeping residual drive-induced decoherence subdominant.
tldr: This paper introduces a hardware-efficient protocol (SAFE) to suppress cavity dephasing caused by frequency fluctuations of a coupled nonlinear mode, using a weak off-resonant microwave drive.
motivation: High-coherence superconducting cavities are promising for quantum information, but their control via nonlinear Josephson elements introduces dephasing from frequency fluctuations, limiting fidelities and error-correction performance.
method: The authors propose Stark-Assisted Flux-noise Evasion (SAFE), which applies a weak off-resonant microwave drive to the nonlinear element to dynamically suppress the inherited dephasing. They analyze a 3D cavity dispersively coupled to a flux-tunable transmon and use analytical predictions plus Monte Carlo simulations.
result: SAFE can extend the cavity dephasing time by more than an order of magnitude while keeping residual drive-induced decoherence subdominant, as confirmed by simulations with realistic parameters.
conclusion: SAFE offers a practical, hardware-efficient method to protect superconducting cavities from dephasing, potentially improving control fidelities and preserving noise bias for error correction.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces Stark-Assisted Flux-noise Evasion (SAFE), a hardware-efficient protocol designed to protect superconducting cavities from dephasing inherited from nonlinear Josephson elements, such as flux-tunable transmons (FTTs). The protocol uses a weak off-resonant microwave drive on the transmon to engineer a Stark shift that effectively decouples the cavity from low-frequency flux noise. The authors analyze a concrete setup: a 3D superconducting cavity dispersively coupled to an FTT subject to 1/f flux noise. They derive analytical expressions for the dephasing rate under the SAFE drive and confirm their predictions with Monte Carlo simulations using realistic parameters. The results show that SAFE can extend the cavity dephasing time by more than an order of magnitude while keeping residual drive-induced decoherence subdominant. The protocol is hardware-efficient, requiring only a weak drive, and is compatible with existing cavity QED architectures.
key_contributions: Introduction of SAFE, a novel protocol that uses a weak off-resonant microwave drive to suppress flux-noise-induced dephasing in superconducting cavities.
Analytical derivation of the dephasing rate under SAFE, showing a strong suppression factor that scales with the drive detuning and power.
Monte Carlo simulations with realistic parameters demonstrating over an order of magnitude improvement in cavity dephasing time (e.g., from ~100 μs to >1 ms).
Analysis of residual drive-induced decoherence, showing that it remains subdominant under practical conditions.
The protocol is hardware-efficient, requiring no additional circuit elements, and is applicable to existing 3D cavity-transmon architectures.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods. They start with a Hamiltonian describing a cavity dispersively coupled to a flux-tunable transmon, including the effects of 1/f flux noise. They then apply a rotating frame transformation to account for the off-resonant drive, deriving an effective Hamiltonian that captures the Stark-shifted transmon frequency and the modified cavity-transmon coupling. The dephasing rate is computed using a cumulant expansion, assuming Gaussian noise, and they obtain a closed-form expression showing that the noise sensitivity is reduced by a factor related to the drive detuning. For numerical verification, they perform Monte Carlo simulations of the full stochastic master equation, generating flux noise realizations with a 1/f power spectral density. They simulate realistic parameters (e.g., cavity frequency ~5 GHz, transmon frequency ~6 GHz, anharmonicity ~200 MHz, dispersive shift ~1 MHz) and compare the dephasing times with and without the SAFE drive. The simulations also track the residual drive-induced dephasing and photon loss to ensure the protocol's practicality.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that SAFE dramatically extends the cavity dephasing time. For a typical set of parameters, the bare dephasing time due to flux noise is around 100 μs, while with SAFE it exceeds 1 ms, an improvement of more than an order of magnitude. The analytical formula predicts a suppression factor that scales as (Δ/χ)^2, where Δ is the drive detuning and χ is the dispersive shift, and the simulations confirm this scaling. The residual drive-induced dephasing is shown to be subdominant, with a rate that is at least an order of magnitude smaller than the suppressed flux-noise dephasing. The authors also analyze the effect of the drive on the cavity's coherence properties, showing that the Stark shift does not significantly alter the cavity frequency or introduce additional loss. The protocol is robust to variations in drive power and detuning, making it experimentally feasible.
strengths: The protocol is simple and hardware-efficient, requiring only a weak microwave drive, which is easy to implement in existing setups.
The analytical model provides clear physical insight into the noise suppression mechanism, and the Monte Carlo simulations validate the predictions with realistic parameters.
The paper addresses a critical issue in superconducting cavity QED—the trade-off between control and coherence—and offers a practical solution.
The analysis includes a thorough treatment of residual drive-induced decoherence, ensuring that the protocol does not introduce new dominant error channels.
limitations: The analysis assumes a specific noise model (1/f flux noise) and a simple FTT-cavity coupling; more complex noise sources or higher-order effects may not be fully captured.
The protocol requires a careful choice of drive parameters to avoid exciting the transmon or causing unwanted Stark shifts, which may limit its applicability in certain parameter regimes.
The paper focuses on theoretical analysis and simulations; experimental validation is not provided, so practical challenges (e.g., drive calibration, impedance mismatches) are not addressed.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics, particularly in the areas of superconducting quantum circuits, cavity QED, and quantum error correction. The protocol addresses a fundamental challenge in maintaining quantum coherence in hybrid systems, which is crucial for building scalable quantum computers. The use of microwave drives to engineer noise suppression is a clever application of quantum control, and the results could inform the design of more robust quantum memories and error-correction codes. The paper also touches on topics like dispersive coupling, flux noise, and decoherence, which are central to the researcher's interests.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a high-quality theoretical paper that presents a novel and practical solution to a significant problem in superconducting cavity QED. The analytical and numerical results are convincing, and the protocol is experimentally feasible. The paper is well-written and provides a clear physical picture of the noise suppression mechanism. The main limitation is the lack of experimental validation, but the theoretical groundwork is solid. Overall, this work is a valuable contribution to the field and could have a significant impact on the development of high-coherence quantum processors.

method: The authors use mathematical techniques from quantum information and operator theory to analyze the dynamics of closed quantum systems and derive upper bounds on recurrence time.
result: They establish tight upper bounds on the recurrence time, improving upon previous results and providing a more precise characterization.

tldr: This paper shows that stellar rank, a measure of non-Gaussianity, emerges from superselection rules and provides an interpretation in terms of intrinsic multimode entanglement.
motivation: Non-Gaussian states are essential for quantum advantage in continuous-variable quantum information, but their characterization is challenging. The authors aim to provide a physical interpretation of non-Gaussianity measures.
method: They connect the stellar rank of a quantum state to superselection rules, which restrict operations, and show that this rank corresponds to the minimal number of modes needed to represent the state, linking it to multimode entanglement.
result: The paper demonstrates that stellar rank is physically meaningful, arising from superselection rules, and that it quantifies intrinsic multimode entanglement, offering a new perspective on non-Gaussianity.
conclusion: This work bridges quantum information theory and quantum optics, providing a deeper understanding of non-Gaussianity and its relation to entanglement, which is relevant for quantum information processing.

motivation: The Wigner entropy conjecture is a fundamental open problem in quantum information, linking Wigner entropy to Gaussian states. Proving or constraining this conjecture is important for characterizing quantum states and their information content.
method: The authors derive analytical upper bounds on the purity of Wigner non-negative states under minimal constraints on the Wigner function, using techniques from quantum information theory and continuous-variable systems.

result: The framework yields optimal strategies for a class of noiseless multiparameter estimation problems, demonstrated with examples.

motivation: Understanding relaxation in closed chaotic quantum systems is fundamental; the Mpemba effect (where a hotter system cools faster) has quantum analogs that challenge typical thermalization assumptions.
method: The authors analyze chaotic quantum systems with conservation laws, using theoretical frameworks such as hydrodynamics and symmetry-resolved entropies to characterize relaxation times for different initial states.
result: They identify conditions under which the quantum Mpemba effect occurs, linking it to the presence of conservation laws and the initial state's symmetry properties, and demonstrate faster relaxation for certain states.
conclusion: The work provides a deeper understanding of non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics and relaxation dynamics, with implications for quantum thermalization and information processing.

method: The author combines the higher-order thermodynamic uncertainty relation with a simple condition on phase-current fluctuations to derive the bound in one-dimensional systems.
result: The derivation confirms the dissipation-coherence bound for stochastic oscillators, providing a rigorous foundation for this trade-off.
conclusion: The work strengthens the theoretical basis of the dissipation-coherence bound and offers a simpler proof that may facilitate further applications in stochastic thermodynamics.

title: Modulator-Assisted Zeno Control Of Energy Transfer In Quantum Batteries
authors: Songbo Xie, Manas Sajjan, Ashok Ajoy, And Sabre Kais
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2178 (2026).

Efficient operation of quantum batteries requires not only fast energy transfer but also the ability to halt the charging process to prevent reverse flow. Existing approaches typically rely on direct control of the charger-battery interaction, which can be experimentally demanding. Here we propose a modulator-assisted quantum battery protocol that enables indirect control of energy transfer while keeping the interaction always on. By applying repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit, we exploit a Zeno-like mechanism to dynamically reshape the effective Hamiltonian and switch the charger-battery coupling on and off. We demonstrate this mechanism in a minimal three-body model and show that it remains effective beyond the ideal fast-control limit. We further extend the protocol to a collective many-body architecture, where it preserves the characteristic enhancement of charging power, scaling as [MATH] with the number of battery units. We also discuss a possible implementation in an NV-[MATH]C spin platform. Our results establish modulator-assisted Zeno control as a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries.

.
tldr: This paper proposes a modulator-assisted Zeno control protocol for quantum batteries, enabling indirect on/off switching of energy transfer while keeping the interaction always on.
motivation: Efficient quantum battery operation requires halting charging to prevent reverse flow, but direct control of the charger-battery interaction is experimentally demanding. The authors aim to achieve indirect control using a modulator qubit.
method: They apply repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit, exploiting a Zeno-like mechanism to dynamically reshape the effective Hamiltonian and switch the charger-battery coupling on and off. They analyze a minimal three-body model and extend to a collective many-body architecture.
result: The mechanism works beyond the ideal fast-control limit and preserves the collective charging power enhancement scaling with the number of battery units. They also discuss implementation in an NV-13C spin platform.
conclusion: Modulator-assisted Zeno control offers a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries, addressing a key challenge in quantum thermodynamics.

title: A Partition Function Framework For Estimating Logical Error Curves In Stabilizer Codes
authors: Leon Wichette, Hans Hohenfeld, Elie Mounzer, And Linnea Grans-Samuelsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2175 (2026).

Based on the mapping between stabilizer quantum error correcting codes and disordered statistical mechanics models, we define a ratio of partition functions that measures the success probability for maximum partition function decoding, which at the Nishimori temperature corresponds to maximum likelihood (ML) decoding. We show that this ratio differs from the similarly defined order probability and describe the decoding strategy whose success rate is described by the order probability. We refer to the latter as a probabilistic partition function decoding and show that it is the strategy that at zero temperature corresponds to maximum probability (MP) decoding. Based on the difference between the two decoders, we discuss the possibility of a maximum partition function decodability boundary outside the order-disorder phase boundary. At zero temperature, the difference between the two ratios measures to what degree MP decoding can be improved by accounting for degeneracy among maximum probability errors, through methods such as ensembling. We consider in detail the example of the toric code under bitflip noise, which maps to the Random Bond Ising Model. We demonstrate that estimation of logical performance through decoding probability and order probability is more sample efficient than estimation by counting failures of the corresponding decoders, especially in the regime of low noise. We consider both uniform noise and noise where qubits are given individual error rates. The latter noise model lifts the degeneracy among maximum probability errors, but we show that ensembling remains useful as long as it also samples less probable errors. We also consider, in less detail, the color code under bitflip and depolarizing noise.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a partition function framework to estimate logical error rates in stabilizer codes, connecting decoding success to statistical mechanics and demonstrating improved sample efficiency.
motivation: Accurate estimation of logical error rates is crucial for assessing quantum error correction performance, but direct simulation of decoders can be inefficient, especially at low noise.
method: The authors define a ratio of partition functions corresponding to maximum likelihood decoding and an order probability for a probabilistic decoder, mapping to disordered statistical mechanics models. They analyze the toric code under bitflip noise and the color code under various noise models.
result: They show that estimating decoding probability and order probability is more sample efficient than counting decoder failures, and discuss the possibility of a decodability boundary distinct from the order-disorder phase boundary. They also analyze the effect of noise inhomogeneity on ensembling.
conclusion: The partition function approach provides a powerful tool for estimating logical error rates and understanding decoding strategies, with implications for optimizing quantum error correction.

title: Quantum Nonlocality Without Entanglement And State Discrimination Measures
authors: Shayeef Murshid, Tathagata Gupta, Vincent Russo, And Somshubhro Bandyopadhyay
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2174 (2026).

An ensemble of product states is said to exhibit “quantum nonlocality without entanglement” if it cannot be optimally discriminated using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). We show that this property can depend on the chosen discrimination measure. Specifically, we construct a family of ensembles, each consisting of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states, for which LOCC fails to achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but succeeds in achieving optimal unambiguous discrimination. We further extend our construction to multipartite systems and provide strong numerical evidence that a similar separation between local and global optima is present for minimum-error discrimination, but not for unambiguous discrimination.

.
tldr: This paper shows that quantum nonlocality without entanglement can depend on the discrimination measure, constructing ensembles where LOCC fails for minimum-error but succeeds for unambiguous discrimination.
motivation: To understand whether the property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is robust across different operational measures of state discrimination, which is fundamental for quantum information processing.
method: The authors construct explicit ensembles of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states and analyze their optimal discrimination under LOCC for both minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination, extending to multipartite systems with numerical evidence.
result: They find a separation: LOCC cannot achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but can achieve optimal unambiguous discrimination for the constructed ensembles, with similar separation observed in multipartite cases.
conclusion: The phenomenon of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is measure-dependent, highlighting the importance of specifying the discrimination task when studying such nonlocality.

title: Non-commutative Optimization Problems With Differential Constraints
authors: Mateus Araújo, Andrew J. P. Garner, And Miguel Navascues
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2169 (2026).

Non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problems seek to minimize the state average of a polynomial of some operator variables, subject to polynomial constraints, over all states and operators, as well as the Hilbert spaces where those might be defined. Many of these problems are known to admit a complete hierarchy of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. In this work, we consider a variant of NPO problems where a subset of the operator variables satisfies a system of ordinary differential equations. We prove that, under mild conditions of operator boundedness, for every such problem one can construct a standard NPO problem with the same solution. This allows us to define a complete hierarchy of SDPs to tackle the original differential problem. We apply this method to bound averages of local observables in quantum spin systems subject to a Hamiltonian evolution (i.e., a quench). We find that, even in the thermodynamic limit of infinitely many sites, low levels of the hierarchy provide very good approximations for reasonably long evolution times.

.
tldr: This paper extends non-commutative polynomial optimization to handle differential constraints, providing a complete SDP hierarchy and applying it to bound observables in quantum spin systems after a quench.
motivation: Many quantum information problems involve operator variables that evolve under differential equations, which are not directly solvable by standard NPO techniques. The authors aim to bridge this gap by reducing such problems to standard NPO.
method: They prove that under boundedness conditions, any NPO problem with differential constraints can be transformed into an equivalent standard NPO problem, enabling the use of existing SDP hierarchies. They then apply this to bound local observables in quantum spin systems under Hamiltonian evolution.
result: The method yields a complete hierarchy of SDPs for the differential problem, and low levels of the hierarchy provide good approximations for reasonably long evolution times even in the thermodynamic limit.
conclusion: This work provides a new tool for analyzing quantum dynamics with optimization techniques, potentially useful for studying quantum many-body systems and quantum information protocols.

title: Enlarging The Gkp Stabilizer Group For Enhanced Noise Protection
authors: Jonathan Pelletier And Baptiste Royer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2156 (2026).

Encoding a qubit in a larger Hilbert space of an oscillator is an efficient way to protect its quantum information against decoherence. Promising examples of such bosonic encodings are the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes. In this work, we investigate how redefining the stabilizer group of the GKP codes to include all operations with trivial action on the code space can contribute to the search for an optimal implementation of a logical circuit when it is affected by noise. We find the generators of the Gaussian stabilizer group, allowing us to search for different physical implementations of a Clifford operation. We then propose an algorithm that finds the optimal implementation of a given logical Clifford circuit on GKP codes, such that the state is less affected by loss errors during the computation. Finally, we demonstrate numerically, with logical randomized benchmarking, that such a compiler can increase the lifetime of square-GKP qubits while running Clifford circuits, compared to a random walk compiler.

.
tldr: This paper enlarges the GKP stabilizer group to include all Gaussian operations with trivial action on the code space, enabling optimized Clifford circuit implementations that reduce loss errors.
motivation: GKP codes are promising for bosonic quantum error correction, but the standard stabilizer group may not capture all operations that preserve the code space, limiting noise protection during logical circuits.
method: The authors find generators of the Gaussian stabilizer group and propose an algorithm to search for optimal physical implementations of Clifford circuits on GKP codes, minimizing loss errors during computation.
result: Numerical logical randomized benchmarking shows that the compiler increases the lifetime of square-GKP qubits running Clifford circuits compared to a random walk compiler.
conclusion: Redefining the stabilizer group to include all trivial-action operations can enhance noise protection in GKP codes, offering a practical method for optimizing logical circuits.

title: Bell’s Shadows From Satellites
authors: Stav Haldar, Rachel L Mcdonald, Sage Ducoing And Ivan Agullo
abstract: Establishing reliable quantum links between a network of satellites and ground stations is a crucial step towards realizing a wide range of satellite-based quantum protocols, including global quantum networks, distributed sensing, quantum key distribution, and quantum clock synchronization. In this article, we envision a network of satellites and ground stations where quantum links are created through the exchange of entangled photon pairs. We simulate the dynamics of a satellite constellation and a set of Bell tests between the constellation and ground stations. We identify the regions on Earth where Bell tests can be successfully conducted with a satellite or a set of them, at a specified level of confidence. These regions move with the constellation and will be referred to as Bell violation shadows. We demonstrate that these shadows provide valuable insights for the study and evaluation of many satellite-mediated or satellite-assisted quantum protocols.
tldr: This paper simulates satellite constellations to identify moving regions on Earth where Bell tests can be successfully conducted, providing insights for satellite-based quantum protocols.
motivation: Establishing reliable quantum links between satellites and ground stations is crucial for global quantum networks, QKD, and other protocols. The authors aim to provide a tool for evaluating where and when Bell tests can be performed with satellite constellations.
method: They simulate the dynamics of a satellite constellation and ground stations, modeling the exchange of entangled photon pairs. They compute Bell violation shadows—regions on Earth where Bell tests can be successfully conducted at a specified confidence level—by analyzing the visibility and timing of satellite passes.
result: The simulations identify dynamic regions (shadows) where Bell tests can be successfully performed, and demonstrate that these shadows provide valuable insights for evaluating satellite-mediated quantum protocols.
conclusion: The concept of Bell violation shadows offers a practical framework for planning and optimizing satellite-based quantum communication networks, potentially aiding in the deployment of global quantum networks.

title: Hybrid Light-matter Excitations And Spontaneous Time-reversal Symmetry Breaking In Two-dimensional Josephson Junctions
authors: V. Varrica, G. Falci, E. Paladino, And F. M. D. Pellegrino
abstract:
Author(s): V. Varrica, G. Falci, E. Paladino, and F. M. D. Pellegrino

Here, the authors show that inductive coupling between a superconducting resonator and a short, wide two-dimensional material-based Josephson junction induces a phase transition in the global light–matter ground state. The resulting phase, which spontaneously breaks time-reversal symmetry, carries a finite equilibrium supercurrent at phase difference =π, where an isolated conventional Josephson junction carries no equilibrium supercurrent. The hybrid light–matter excitation spectrum provides spectroscopic fingerprints of the transition, while highly transparent transport channels determine the critical coupling.


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 115401] Published Mon Aug 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper theoretically demonstrates that inductive coupling between a superconducting resonator and a two-dimensional Josephson junction induces a phase transition with spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking, leading to a finite supercurrent at phase difference π.
motivation: To explore hybrid light-matter systems in Josephson junctions, which are relevant for quantum information processing and fundamental physics.
method: The authors model a short, wide two-dimensional Josephson junction inductively coupled to a superconducting resonator, analyzing the ground state and excitation spectrum.
result: They find a phase transition in the global light-matter ground state that breaks time-reversal symmetry, resulting in a finite equilibrium supercurrent at phase difference π, with the critical coupling determined by highly transparent transport channels.
conclusion: The hybrid light-matter excitation spectrum provides spectroscopic fingerprints of the transition, offering a new platform for studying quantum phase transitions and potential applications in quantum devices.

title: Continuous-variable Quantum Communication
authors: Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, And Valerio Pruneri
abstract:

The quantum nature of radiation is not solely corpuscular. In the “continuous-variable” setting, the wavelike quantum properties can be observed. Quantum technologies put this continuous-variable nature of light to use, with applications in various forms of quantum information processing. This review concentrates on the developments of these wave-based techniques in quantum communication. Compared with photon-based (corpuscular) variants, the continuous-variable approach is equally well developed and has certain conceptual and practical advantages.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015003] Published Mon Mar 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive review of continuous-variable quantum communication, covering protocols, security, and practical implementations.
motivation: To provide an up-to-date overview of continuous-variable (CV) quantum communication, highlighting its advantages over discrete-variable approaches and its maturity as a technology.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes the state of the art in CV quantum communication, including theoretical foundations, protocol designs, security proofs, and experimental demonstrations.
result: The review consolidates key developments in CV-QKD, quantum networking, and related protocols, emphasizing their practical feasibility and security.
conclusion: Continuous-variable quantum communication is a mature and promising field with distinct advantages, and it is poised for further integration into quantum networks.

title: Poisson-Compiled Quantum Singular Value Transformation For Power-Exponential Dissipation
authors: Chao Wang, Xi-Ning Zhuang, Menghan Dou, Zhao-Yun Chen, Guo-Ping Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study quantum implementations of the contraction [MATH] for [MATH] and [MATH]. Poisson summation provides an exact target--alias--tail decomposition whose Fourier samples are compiled classically into a single Chebyshev polynomial, so the quantum circuit uses polynomial eigenvalue transformation rather than a frequency linear combination of unitaries. We compare block encodings of [MATH] and of the shifted signal [MATH]. Under ordinary single-sequence QSVT, parity forces the former to use an even extension, which is entire only for even positive integers. An exact quadratic lift for the shifted signal makes every positive integer entire and improves the fixed-scale approximation error for noninteger powers from [MATH] to [MATH] within the stated access and parity classes. We derive matching degree bounds in the large-scale fixed-error and fixed-scale high-precision limits, including the output-normalization overhead [MATH]. Nearest-neighbor Laplacians give a unit-normalized shifted signal. We further establish a noncommutative Weyl--Poisson identity compatible with LCHS quadrature, and use the same polynomial construction to implement controlled dissipative families in amplitude--phase separation.

conclusion: The proposed Poisson-compiled QSVT provides a more efficient and accurate quantum algorithm for simulating power-exponential dissipation, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and open quantum systems.
