Author(s): Mauro E. S. Morales, Lirandë Pira, Philipp Schleich, Kelvin Koor, Pedro C. S. Costa, Dong An, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Lin Lin, Patrick Rebentrost, and Dominic W. Berry

Given vector b and matrix
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025005] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive survey of quantum algorithms for solving linear systems, from HHL to recent developments.
motivation: Solving linear systems is a central computational task, and quantum algorithms offer potential speedups. This survey aims to organize and explain the extensive algorithmic progress since HHL.
method: The paper reviews the HHL algorithm and subsequent post-HHL developments, categorizing techniques such as quantum signal processing, adiabatic approaches, and variational methods.
result: Provides a structured overview of the state of the art in quantum linear system solvers, highlighting key algorithmic ideas and their complexities.
conclusion: The survey consolidates knowledge in this area, serving as a reference for researchers and identifying open challenges.

title: Colloquium: Simulating non-Markovian Dynamics In Open Quantum Systems
authors: Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, And J. Ankerhold
abstract:
Author(s): Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, and J. Ankerhold

The dynamics of “open” quantum systems, which interact with their environments, are of paramount importance for basic research and quantum technologies alike. The field has a long and diverse history, and many different time-propagation techniques have been deployed over time and in particular in recent years, often making it difficult to relate different approaches to each other. Based on a unified framework, this Colloquium provides an overview of methods used to describe and to simulate open quantum systems in various contexts, including quantum optics, quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, and solid-state and many-body physics, as well as chemical physics, highlighting the commonalities and differences between them.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021002] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium provides a unified framework for simulating non-Markovian open quantum systems, covering various methods and their applications across quantum optics, quantum information, thermodynamics, and many-body physics.
motivation: Open quantum systems are crucial for quantum technologies, but non-Markovian dynamics are challenging to simulate. The field has many disparate techniques, making it hard to relate them.
method: The authors present a unified framework that organizes and compares different time-propagation techniques for non-Markovian open quantum systems, highlighting commonalities and differences.
result: The paper offers a comprehensive overview of simulation methods, including their applicability and limitations in various physical contexts.
conclusion: The unified framework helps researchers choose appropriate simulation methods for non-Markovian open quantum systems, advancing both theoretical understanding and practical applications.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: This review explores space-time duality in quantum many-body dynamics, linking brickwork quantum circuits to a unified view of dynamical evolution.
motivation: Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult; the authors aim to provide a pedagogical review of space-time duality as a unifying framework.
method: The paper reviews and synthesizes recent advances in space-time duality, focusing on brickwork quantum circuits and their role in exactly solvable dynamics.
result: It presents a unified perspective on dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems via space-time duality, highlighting connections to quantum computation.
conclusion: Space-time duality offers a powerful tool for understanding and solving quantum many-body dynamics, with implications for quantum simulation and computation.

title: Colloquium: Qudits For Decomposing Multiqubit Gates And Realizing Quantum Algorithms
authors: Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, And Aleksey K. Fedorov
abstract:
Author(s): Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, and Aleksey K. Fedorov

Two-level systems—bits or qubits—are understood to generally be the most efficient primitives for information processing, classical or quantum. But this is not to say that there are no roles to be played by multilevel systems. This Colloquium surveys these possible roles for the quantum case. Here we speak of qudits:
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021003] Published Tue Jun 03, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the use of qudits (multilevel quantum systems) for decomposing multiqubit gates and implementing quantum algorithms, highlighting simplifications like the Toffoli gate with qutrits.
motivation: Qudits offer potential advantages in quantum computing, such as reducing circuit complexity and enabling more efficient gate decompositions, which could be relevant to quantum information processing.
method: The paper surveys various qudit-qubit embeddings, discusses theoretical frameworks for gate decomposition using qudits, and reviews current experimental implementations.
result: It demonstrates that using qudits can drastically simplify certain quantum gates (e.g., Toffoli) and provides an overview of the state of the art in qudit-based quantum computing experiments.
conclusion: Qudits present a promising avenue for quantum computation, though the field is still developing; the review consolidates current knowledge and points to future directions.

title: Entanglement Growth In The Dark Intervals Of A Locally Monitored Free-fermion Chain
authors: Giovanni Di Fresco, Youenn Le Gal, Davide Valenti, Marco Schiró, And Angelo Carollo
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2183 (2026).

We consider a free fermionic chain with monitoring of the particle density on a single site of the chain and study the entanglement dynamics of quantum jump trajectories. We show that the entanglement entropy grows in time towards a stationary state which display volume law scaling of the entropy, in stark contrast with both the unitary dynamics after a local quench and the no-click limit corresponding to full post-selection. We explain the extensive entanglement growth as a consequence of the peculiar distribution of quantum jumps in time, which display superpoissonian waiting time distribution characterised by a bunching of quantum jumps followed by long dark intervals where no-clicks are detected, akin to the distribution of fluorescence light in a driven atom. We show that the presence of dark intervals is the key feature to explain the effect and that by increasing the number of sites which are monitored the volume law scaling gives away to the Zeno effect and its associated area law.

.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement growth in a free-fermion chain under local monitoring, revealing volume-law scaling due to dark intervals in quantum jumps.
motivation: Understanding how measurement-induced dynamics affect entanglement in many-body systems is crucial for quantum information processing and thermodynamics.
method: The authors analyze quantum jump trajectories of a free-fermion chain with single-site density monitoring, deriving waiting time distributions and entanglement entropy scaling.
result: They find super-Poissonian waiting times with bunching and dark intervals, leading to volume-law entanglement, contrasting with unitary and no-click limits; increasing monitored sites induces Zeno effect and area law.
conclusion: Dark intervals are key to extensive entanglement growth, providing insight into measurement-induced phases and quantum thermodynamics.

title: On The Quantum Computational Complexity Of Classical Linear Dynamics With Geometrically Local Interactions: Dequantization And Universality
authors: Kazuki Sakamoto And Keisuke Fujii
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2182 (2026).

The simulation of large-scale classical systems in exponentially small space on quantum computers has gained attention. The prior work demonstrated that a quantum algorithm offers an exponential speedup over any classical algorithm in simulating classical dynamics with long-range interactions. However, many real-world classical systems, such as those arising from partial differential equations, exhibit only local interactions. The question remains whether quantum algorithms can still provide exponential speedup under this condition. In this work, we thoroughly characterize the computational complexity of simulating such geometrically local systems on quantum computers. First, we dequantize the quantum algorithm for simulating short-time (polynomial-time) dynamics of such systems. This implies that the problem of simulating this dynamics does not yield any exponential quantum advantage. Second, we show that simulating short-time dynamics is at least as hard as polynomial-time and linear-space probabilistic classical computation. Third, we show that the computational complexity of simulating long-time (exponential-time) dynamics is captured by exponential-time and polynomial-space quantum computation. This suggests a super-polynomial time advantage when restricting the computation to polynomial-space, or an exponential space advantage otherwise. This work offers new insights into the complexity of classical dynamics governed by partial differential equations, providing a pathway for achieving quantum advantage in practical problems.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the quantum computational complexity of simulating classical linear dynamics with geometrically local interactions, showing no exponential quantum advantage for short-time dynamics but potential super-polynomial advantage for long-time dynamics under space constraints.
motivation: To determine whether quantum computers can provide exponential speedup for simulating classical systems with local interactions, which are common in real-world applications like partial differential equations.
method: The authors dequantize the quantum algorithm for short-time dynamics, prove hardness results for short-time simulation, and analyze the complexity of long-time dynamics in terms of quantum complexity classes.
result: Short-time dynamics simulation has no exponential quantum advantage and is as hard as polynomial-time linear-space probabilistic classical computation; long-time dynamics is captured by exponential-time polynomial-space quantum computation, suggesting super-polynomial time advantage under space restrictions.
conclusion: The work provides a thorough complexity characterization, offering insights into when quantum advantage may be achievable for simulating classical dynamics with local interactions.

title: Entanglement-assisted Quasi-cyclic Quantum Low-density Parity-check Codes Over Qubits
authors: Pavan Kumar, Abhi Kumar Sharma, Karthik Bharadwaj, And Shayan Srinivasa Garani
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2181 (2026).

We construct several families of entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC (EA-QC-QLDPC) codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices. The entanglement-unassisted portion of the joint Tanner graph of the proposed EA-QC-QLDPC code derived from two distinct classical QC-LDPC codes is free of 4-cycles. Notably, one of the proposed families constructed from two distinct classical codes requires only a [MATH] shared Bell pair between the quantum transmitter and receiver, highlighting its resource efficiency. We also analytically determine the exact code rates for some of the proposed constructions. Furthermore, two of the proposed families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes are derived from a single classical code whose Tanner graphs possess girth greater than six, further enhancing their error-correcting performance. We also propose an encoding scheme with improved complexity by exploiting the proposed code structure. The performance of the proposed codes is assessed under both random and burst error models under the depolarizing and Markovian noise actions. Simulation results reveal nearly one order of improvement in error-correction performance with the quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum (QBLNMS) decoder compared to the layered binary sum-product decoder over both depolarizing and Markovian channels. Using the QBLNMS decoder over a quaternary alphabet, we demonstrate that correlated Pauli errors can be effectively handled within the decoding framework. Furthermore, under the QBLNMS decoding, the proposed codes achieve [MATH] performance improvements compared to prior works and can effectively handle both random and burst errors. The code constructions are scalable across various coding rates and quantum payloads, crucial for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

.
tldr: This paper constructs entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC codes with improved error-correction performance and resource efficiency.
motivation: Quantum error correction is essential for reliable quantum communication and computation, and constructing efficient quantum LDPC codes with good performance is a key challenge.
method: The authors construct EA-QC-QLDPC codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices, ensuring 4-cycle-free Tanner graphs and deriving exact code rates. They also propose an encoding scheme and evaluate performance using QBLNMS and layered binary sum-product decoders.
result: The proposed codes achieve nearly an order of magnitude improvement in error-correction performance with QBLNMS decoder over depolarizing and Markovian channels, and require only one shared Bell pair for one family.
conclusion: The scalable constructions and improved decoding demonstrate practical potential for quantum communication and computing systems.

title: Pilot-Wave Simulator: Exact Classical Sampling From Ideal And Noisy Quantum Circuits Up To Hundreds Of Qubits
authors: Gleb Kalachev, Pavel Mosharev, Zuoheng Zou, Pavel Panteleev, And Man-Hong Yung
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2173 (2026).

Quantum circuit simulators running on classical computers offer a vital platform for designing, testing, and optimizing quantum algorithms, driving innovation despite limited access to real quantum hardware. However, their scalability is inherently constrained by exponential memory and computational overhead, which restricts accurate simulation of large-scale quantum circuits and often results in approximate output distributions. Here, we propose an exact sampling algorithm that integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, wherein a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. As a demonstration, we target the challenge of generating samples from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating both depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models. These results enable further validation of several assumptions and conjectures at a scale previously out of reach, significantly expanding the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research.

.
tldr: This paper presents an exact classical sampling algorithm for quantum circuits up to hundreds of qubits by combining tensor network contraction with a Markov process, demonstrated on QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits under noise.
motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is limited by exponential overhead, and approximate methods are often insufficient. The authors aim to provide an exact sampling method that scales to larger circuits, enabling validation of quantum algorithms and noise models.
method: The algorithm integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, where a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. This allows exact sampling from the output distribution of ideal and noisy circuits.
result: The method successfully generates samples from QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models, achieving a scale previously out of reach for exact simulation.
conclusion: The work significantly expands the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research, providing a tool to validate assumptions and conjectures at larger scales, which is relevant to quantum information processing.

title: Hoare Meets Heisenberg: A Lightweight Logic For Quantum Programs
authors: Aarthi Sundaram, Robert Rand, Kartik Singhal, Youngchan Cho, And Brad Lackey
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2172 (2026).

We show that Gottesman's (1998) semantics for Clifford circuits based on the Heisenberg representation gives rise to a lightweight Hoare-like logic for efficiently characterizing a common subset of quantum programs. Our applications include (i) certifying whether auxiliary qubits can be safely disposed of, (ii) determining if a system is separable across a given bipartition, (iii) checking the transversality of a gate with respect to a given stabilizer code, and (iv) computing post-measurement states for computational basis measurements. Further, this logic is extended to accommodate universal quantum computing by deriving Hoare triples for the [MATH]-gate, multiply-controlled unitaries such as the Toffoli gate, and some gate injection circuits that use associated magic states. A number of interesting results emerge from this logic, including a lower bound on the number of [MATH] gates necessary to perform a multiply-controlled [MATH] gate.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a lightweight Hoare-like logic for quantum programs based on Gottesman's Heisenberg semantics, enabling efficient certification of properties like qubit disposal, separability, and gate transversality.
motivation: To provide a practical, lightweight verification method for quantum programs, leveraging stabilizer formalism to reason about a common subset of quantum computations.
method: The authors formalize a Hoare logic using Gottesman's Heisenberg representation for Clifford circuits, then extend it to universal quantum computing via derived Hoare triples for non-Clifford gates and magic states.
result: The logic enables efficient certification of auxiliary qubit disposal, bipartite separability, gate transversality, and post-measurement states, and yields a lower bound on T-gates for multiply-controlled gates.
conclusion: The proposed logic offers a scalable verification tool for quantum programs, with potential applications in quantum error correction and resource management.

title: Optimal Schedule Of Multi-channel Quantum Zeno Dragging With Application To Solving The k-SAT Problem
authors: Yipei Zhang, Alain Sarlette, Philippe Lewalle, Tathagata Karmakar, Thilo Scharnhorst, And K. Birgitta Whaley
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2167 (2026).

Quantum Zeno dragging enables the preparation of common eigenstates of a set of observables by frequent measurement and adiabatic-like modulation of the measurement basis. In this work, we present a deeper analysis of multi-channel Zeno dragging using generalized measurements, i.e. simultaneously measuring a set of non-commuting observables that vary slowly in time, to drag the state towards a target subspace. For concreteness, we will focus on a measurement-driven approach to solving k-SAT problems as examples. We first compute some analytical upper bounds on the convergence time, including the effect of finite measurement time resolution. We then apply optimal control theory to obtain the optimal dragging schedule that lower bounds the convergence time, for low-dimensional settings. This study provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and its optimization, and also serves as a guide for designing optimal dragging schedules for quantum information tasks including measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes multi-channel quantum Zeno dragging with generalized measurements and applies optimal control to find schedules that minimize convergence time for solving k-SAT problems.
motivation: Quantum Zeno dragging can prepare target states via frequent measurements, but multi-channel versions with non-commuting observables lack rigorous analysis and optimization, especially for practical tasks like solving k-SAT.
method: The authors derive analytical upper bounds on convergence time, including finite measurement resolution effects, and use optimal control theory to compute optimal dragging schedules in low-dimensional settings.
result: They provide theoretical bounds and demonstrate that optimal schedules can lower the convergence time compared to naive approaches, with examples for k-SAT.
conclusion: The work establishes a foundation for optimizing multi-channel Zeno dragging, offering guidance for measurement-driven quantum algorithms and quantum information tasks.

title: Geometric Speed Limit Of State Preparation And Curved Control Spaces
authors: Maximilian Goll And Robert H. Jonsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2160 (2026).

The preparation of quantum many-body systems faces the difficulty that in a realistic scenario only few control parameters of the system may be accessible. In this context, an interesting connection between the energy fluctuations during state preparation and its geometric length as measured by the Fubini-Study metric was discussed by Bukov et al. in 2019 [5]. An inspiring conjecture lower bounding the energy fluctuations by the minimal geometric length of all accessible state preparation protocols was put forward together with supporting examples and numerical evidence. However, we here show that the conjecture does not hold but can be violated if the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature, when embedded into the space of all dynamically accessible states. We illustrate this by a number of generic qubit, qutrit and harmonic oscillator systems.

.
tldr: This paper disproves a conjecture on geometric speed limits for state preparation by showing violations in systems with curved control spaces.
motivation: The authors aim to test a conjecture that energy fluctuations during state preparation are lower bounded by the minimal geometric length of accessible protocols, which would have implications for quantum control and thermodynamics.
method: They analyze qubit, qutrit, and harmonic oscillator systems, demonstrating that the conjecture fails when the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature.
result: They provide counterexamples where energy fluctuations are smaller than the conjectured bound, highlighting the role of curvature in control landscapes.
conclusion: The conjecture is not universally valid, and geometric speed limits must account for the curvature of the control space.

title: Near-Optimal Parameter Tuning Of Level-1 Qaoa For Ising Models
authors: V Vijendran, Dax Enshan Koh, Eunok Bae, Hyukjoon Kwon, Ping Koy Lam, And Syed M Assad
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2158 (2026).

The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) tackles combinatorial optimisation problems by encoding their solutions into the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian prepared by a [MATH]-level parameterised circuit, with the angles tuned classically. Parameter optimisation is widely regarded as a central bottleneck, even for the shallowest circuits. Focusing on QAOA at [MATH] (QAOA[MATH]), we show that tuning the two angles [MATH] for weighted Ising models is not a black-box search but a structured signal-processing problem. We prove that the QAOA[MATH] expectation value is a partial Fourier series in [MATH] whose frequencies are determined explicitly by the problem's couplings and fields, giving instance-wise bandwidth bounds and, via the Nyquist–Shannon theorem, the sampling resolution needed to avoid the aliasing that causes coarse-grid searches to return spurious optima. We then eliminate the mixer angle analytically, computing [MATH] in closed form to reduce the search to one dimension, and apply a subdivision algorithm that locates the globally optimal [MATH] in polynomial time with a certificate of optimality when the weights are commensurable and bounded. For regular weighted graphs, we further prove the conventional wisdom that the globally optimal [MATH] concentrates near zero and coincides with the first local optimum, giving a rigorous account of the empirical success of small-angle initialisation and allowing gradient descent to replace exhaustive line searches. Validated within Recursive QAOA (RQAOA) on weighted instances of 128 and 256 qubits, our method consistently outperforms both coarsely optimised RQAOA and semidefinite programming.

.
tldr: This paper provides a rigorous analysis of QAOA parameter optimization for Ising models, showing that the expectation value is a partial Fourier series and deriving optimal sampling and initialization strategies.
motivation: Parameter optimization is a central bottleneck in QAOA, and the authors aim to replace black-box search with a structured signal-processing approach.
method: They prove the QAOA1 expectation value is a partial Fourier series with frequencies determined by problem couplings, use Nyquist-Shannon to determine sampling resolution, eliminate the mixer angle analytically, and apply a subdivision algorithm for global optimization.
result: They provide polynomial-time global optimization with optimality certificates for commensurable weights, prove concentration of optimal angles near zero for regular graphs, and validate on RQAOA for 128 and 256 qubits, outperforming coarse optimization and SDP.
conclusion: QAOA parameter tuning can be understood and solved more efficiently than previously thought, with implications for practical quantum optimization.

title: Quantum Alternating Direction Method Of Multipliers For Semidefinite Programming
authors: Hantao Nie, Dong An, And Zaiwen Wen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2154 (2026).

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a fundamental convex optimization problem with wide-ranging applications. However, solving large-scale instances remains computationally challenging due to the high cost of solving linear systems and performing eigenvalue decompositions. In this paper, we present a quantum alternating direction method of multipliers (QADMM) for SDPs, building on recent advances in quantum computing. An inexact ADMM framework is developed, which tolerates errors in the iterates arising from block-encoding approximation and quantum measurement. Within this robust scheme, we design a polynomial proximal operator to address the semidefinite conic constraints and apply the quantum singular value transformation to accelerate the most costly projection updates. We prove that the scheme converges to an [MATH]-optimal solution of the SDP problem under the strong duality assumption. A detailed complexity analysis shows that the QADMM algorithm achieves favorable scaling with respect to dimension compared to the classical ADMM algorithm and quantum interior point methods, highlighting its potential for solving large-scale SDPs.

.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum alternating direction method of multipliers (QADMM) for solving semidefinite programming problems, leveraging quantum singular value transformation and an inexact ADMM framework.
motivation: Large-scale SDPs are computationally challenging due to costly linear system solves and eigenvalue decompositions; quantum computing may offer speedups.
method: The authors develop an inexact ADMM that tolerates errors from block-encoding and measurement, use a polynomial proximal operator for the semidefinite cone, and apply quantum singular value transformation to accelerate projections.
result: They prove convergence to an ε-optimal solution under strong duality and provide complexity analysis showing favorable scaling in dimension compared to classical ADMM and quantum interior point methods.
conclusion: The QADMM algorithm demonstrates potential for solving large-scale SDPs with quantum advantage, though practical implementation remains challenging.

title: Sparse Identification Of Quantum Hamiltonian Dynamics Via Quantum Circuit Learning
authors: Yusei Tateyama And Yuzuru Kato
abstract: Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) is a data-driven framework for estimating classical nonlinear dynamical systems from time-series data. In this approach, system dynamics is represented as a linear combination of a predefined set of basis functions, and the corresponding coefficients are sparsely estimated from observed time-series data. In this study, we propose sparse identification of quantum Hamiltonian dynamics (SIQHDy), a SINDy-inspired quantum circuit learning framework for estimating quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from time-series data of quantum measurement outcomes. In SIQHDy, the unitary evolution of a quantum Hamiltonian system is expressed as a product of basis quantum circuits, and the corresponding circuit parameters are estimated through sparsity-promoting optimization. We numerically demonstrate that SIQHDy accurately reconstructs the dynamics of single-, three-, and five-spin systems, and exhibits robustness to measurement noise in the three-spin case. Furthermore, we propose an extension of SIQHDy for scenarios with limited accessible observables and evaluate its performance in identifying three-spin systems and in network-structure identification for five-spin systems.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum circuit learning framework inspired by SINDy to sparsely identify quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from measurement time-series data.
motivation: Estimating quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from data is crucial for characterizing quantum systems, but existing methods may require many measurements or prior knowledge. The authors aim to provide a data-driven approach that leverages sparsity to efficiently reconstruct the Hamiltonian.
method: The method, SIQHDy, represents the unitary evolution as a product of basis quantum circuits and estimates the circuit parameters via sparsity-promoting optimization, using time-series data of quantum measurement outcomes. An extension handles limited accessible observables.
result: Numerical demonstrations show accurate reconstruction for single-, three-, and five-spin systems, with robustness to measurement noise in the three-spin case. The extension also performs well in identifying three-spin systems and network structures for five-spin systems.
conclusion: SIQHDy offers a promising data-driven tool for quantum Hamiltonian identification, with potential applications in quantum system characterization and network inference.

title: Rotation-enhanced Photonic Spin Hall Effect In A Ring Bose–Einstein Condensate
authors: Leibo Deng, Muqaddar Abbas, Ghaisud Din, Hocine Bahlouli And Yong-Hong Ma
abstract: We show that rotation can strongly amplify the photonic spin Hall effect in a ring Bose–Einstein condensate. For an incident probe beam carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM), the spin-dependent transverse shift of the reflected light is weak in the non-rotating regime but becomes strongly enhanced under rotation because rotation lifts the degeneracy of the condensate mechanical modes via Bragg scattering. The resulting mode splitting produces large photonic spin Hall shifts at ultra-low optical power, with the enhancement increasing with both the condensate winding number and the probe OAM , while remaining weakly affected by atom–atom interactions. Our findings elucidate a rotation-governed mechanism underlying spin-dependent light transport in hybrid atom–optomechanical systems, thereby highlighting its potential for applications in high-precision rotational sensing.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that rotation can strongly enhance the photonic spin Hall effect in a ring Bose-Einstein condensate, enabling large spin-dependent shifts at ultra-low optical power.
motivation: The photonic spin Hall effect is typically weak, limiting its applications. The authors aim to find a mechanism to amplify it, potentially for high-precision rotational sensing.
method: They theoretically analyze a ring Bose-Einstein condensate coupled to an optical cavity, considering Bragg scattering and mechanical mode degeneracy lifted by rotation. They compute the spin-dependent transverse shift of reflected probe light carrying orbital angular momentum.
result: Rotation induces mode splitting that greatly enhances the photonic spin Hall shift, with enhancement increasing with condensate winding number and probe OAM, while being weakly affected by atom-atom interactions.
conclusion: The rotation-governed mechanism provides a new way to control spin-dependent light transport in hybrid atom-optomechanical systems, with potential for high-precision rotational sensing.

title: Fate Of Entanglement In Open Quantum Spin Liquid: Time Evolution Of Its Genuine Multipartite Negativity Upon Sudden Coupling To A Dissipative Bosonic Environment
authors: Federico Garcia-Gaitan And Branislav K Nikolić
abstract: Many-body entanglement properties of quantum spin liquids (QSLs), persisting at arbitrarily long distances, have been intensely explored over the past two decades, but mostly for QSLs viewed as closed quantum systems. However, in experiments and potential quantum computing applications, candidate materials for this exotic phase of quantum matter will always interact with a dissipative environment, such as the one generated by bosonic quasiparticles in solids at finite temperature. Here we investigate both the stability and spatial distribution of entanglement for the Kitaev model of QSL, which is made open by its sudden coupling to an infinite bosonic bath of Caldeira–Leggett type and then time-evolved in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. From the time-dependent density matrix of QSL subregions, we extract genuine multipartite negativity (GMN), quantum Fisher information, spin–spin correlators, and the expectation value (EV) of the Wilson loop operator. In particular, time dependence of GMN offers the most penetrating insights: (i) in the Markovian regime, it remains nonzero only in hexagonal loopy subregions of QSL (as also discovered very recently for closed QSLs), eventually vanishing on the same timescale on which the EV of the Wilson loop operator vanishes; (ii) in the non-Markovian regime with pronounced memory effects, surprisingly, GMN remains nonzero up to much higher temperatures. In addition, the non-Markovian dynamics generates emergent interactions between spins, thereby opening avenues for tailoring properties of QSL via engineering of dissipation.
tldr: This paper studies the time evolution of genuine multipartite negativity in an open Kitaev quantum spin liquid coupled to a dissipative bosonic environment, revealing that non-Markovian dynamics preserves entanglement at higher temperatures.
motivation: Quantum spin liquids are typically studied as closed systems, but real materials interact with dissipative environments. Understanding how entanglement in QSLs behaves under open system dynamics is crucial for quantum computing applications.
method: The authors model the Kitaev QSL coupled to a Caldeira-Leggett bosonic bath and simulate time evolution in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. They compute genuine multipartite negativity, quantum Fisher information, spin-spin correlators, and Wilson loop expectation values from the time-dependent density matrix.
result: In the Markovian regime, GMN remains nonzero only in hexagonal loopy subregions and vanishes on the same timescale as the Wilson loop. In the non-Markovian regime, GMN persists up to much higher temperatures, and non-Markovian dynamics induces emergent spin-spin interactions.
conclusion: The findings suggest that engineered dissipation can tailor QSL properties, and non-Markovian effects can enhance entanglement stability, which is relevant for quantum information processing in open systems.

title: On The Interpretation Of Hahn Echo Measurements In Electron Spin Resonance Scanning Tunneling Microscopy
authors: Paul Greule, Wantong Huang, Máté Stark, Kwan Ho Au-Yeung, Christoph Wolf, Soo-Hyon Phark, Andreas J Heinrich And Philip Willke
abstract: Electron spin resonance scanning tunneling microscopy (ESR-STM) has become a powerful tool for probing spin dynamics and coherence of individual atoms and molecules on surfaces. In this work, we perform Rabi oscillation and Hahn echo pulse protocols on individual iron phthalocyanine (FePc) molecules on MgO/Ag(001) using ESR-STM. While Hahn echo protocols are widely used to extract spin coherence times, we show that in ESR-STM they are particularly susceptible to misinterpretation due to tunneling electrons generated by the applied radio-frequency (RF) and direct current (DC) voltage. The RF voltage not only drives the spin, but simultaneously probes and relaxes it in combination with the constant DC readout. This consequently leads to an exponential decay that reflects spin relaxation ( ) rather than intrinsic phase coherence ( ). We moreover show that varying both delay times in the refocusing pulse sequence is a reliable way to ensure a coherent nature of the echo signal. The extracted decay for the latter protocol suggests that is and is thus closer to the decoherence time observed in Rabi oscillation measurements. This is significantly shorter than values reported in previous echo measurements. Our findings underscore the need for caution in interpreting times from Hahn echo and Carr-Purcell protocols in ESR-STM and provide practical criteria for distinguishing true spin echoes from tunneling-induced relaxometry signals.
tldr: This paper investigates Hahn echo measurements in ESR-STM on FePc molecules, showing that the measured decay often reflects spin relaxation rather than coherence, and proposes a method to distinguish true echoes.
motivation: ESR-STM is a powerful tool for probing spin coherence, but Hahn echo protocols may be misinterpreted due to tunneling electrons. The authors aim to clarify the interpretation and provide reliable criteria for extracting coherence times.
method: They perform Rabi oscillation and Hahn echo pulse protocols on individual FePc molecules on MgO/Ag(001) using ESR-STM, varying delay times in the refocusing pulse sequence to test the coherence nature of the echo signal.
result: They find that the exponential decay in Hahn echo measurements often reflects spin relaxation (T1) rather than intrinsic phase coherence (T2). Varying both delay times reveals a coherent echo, yielding a T2 closer to the decoherence time from Rabi oscillations, significantly shorter than previously reported.
conclusion: The findings underscore the need for caution in interpreting T2 times from Hahn echo and Carr-Purcell protocols in ESR-STM, and provide practical criteria for distinguishing true spin echoes from tunneling-induced relaxometry signals.

title: Structured Light Under Turbulence
authors: Guilherme S. Barros, Lucas C. C\'eleri, Antonio Zelaquett Khoury, Andr\'e L. S. Santos Junior, Rafael M. Gomes, Guilherme L. Zanin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structured light has emerged as a promising resource for high-capacity and secure free-space optical communication, where atmospheric turbulence remains a major source of signal degradation. In this work, we investigate the resilience of different transverse mode structures of an optical beam with respect to the random action of turbulence. A spatial light modulator (SLM) is programmed to apply amplitude and phase modulation corresponding to the desired transverse mode, which is then transmitted through a turbulent medium emulated by a second SLM. Laguerre-Gauss, Hermite-Gauss, and Airy beams are investigated through the resulting intensity distributions measured with a camera. Different figures of merit are used to evaluate and compare the resilience of these modes.
tldr: This paper experimentally compares the resilience of different structured light modes (Laguerre-Gauss, Hermite-Gauss, Airy) under simulated atmospheric turbulence using spatial light modulators.
motivation: Structured light is promising for high-capacity free-space optical communication, but atmospheric turbulence degrades the beam. The authors aim to identify which transverse mode structures are most resilient to turbulence.
method: They program one SLM to generate the desired transverse mode, transmit it through a turbulent medium emulated by a second SLM, and measure the resulting intensity distributions with a camera. They use multiple figures of merit to compare the modes.
result: The paper reports comparative resilience of the different modes under turbulence, though specific quantitative results are not provided in the abstract.
conclusion: The findings may guide the choice of structured light modes for robust free-space optical communication, but the work is primarily experimental and applied, with limited new theoretical insight.

title: Photon Localization: A Comparative Study
authors: Laura M. Ferguson, Ricardo Rojas Castellano, Kayla Oltman, Joshua G. Fenwick, Rainer Dick
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We compare different measures for photon localization in terms of two-dimensional Gaussian wave packets. We find that all measures start to coalesce if the wave packet has evolved for times which are larger than a few times the inverse momentum-space width of the package. However, the Landau-Peierls wave function yields the largest positive offset -ct>0 while the scalar Fourier transform of the wave packet yields the smallest offset and converges towards -ct=0 fastest. We also discuss local detection of photons through a model detector consisting of ions in ion traps. The position-dependent detection probabilities are inferred from the scattering matrix. We find that the local detection probability for photons can be expressed in terms of three of the proposed localization measures, viz. the Landau-Peierls wave function, the energy wave function, and the Hawton density. Those three porposals also remain close throughout the time evolution of the single-photon wave packet.
tldr: This paper compares different measures of photon localization and discusses local detection via ion traps, but it is not directly aligned with the core research interests.
motivation: To understand which photon localization measures are most appropriate for describing single-photon wave packets and to relate them to local detection probabilities.
method: The authors compare several localization measures (e.g., Landau-Peierls wave function, energy wave function, Hawton density) for two-dimensional Gaussian wave packets, and model a detector using ions in traps to compute position-dependent detection probabilities from the scattering matrix.
result: All measures coalesce after sufficient evolution, but the Landau-Peierls wave function gives the largest positive offset, while the scalar Fourier transform converges fastest to -ct=0. The local detection probability can be expressed in terms of three of the proposed measures.
conclusion: The study provides insights into photon localization measures and their connection to local detection, but it is more of a comparative analysis than a novel contribution to quantum information theory.

title: Efficient Depth--Ancilla Tradeoffs For Hamming Weight Computation And Symmetric Boolean Functions
authors: Wei Zi, Pei Yuan, Junhong Nie, Shengyu Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hamming weight computation maps an [MATH]-bit input to the number of ones it contains. It is a basic subroutine in quantum computing, and the core building block for symmetric Boolean functions, whose value depends only on the Hamming weight of the input. Moreover, symmetric Boolean functions are among the most common primitives in quantum computing. Efficient circuits for both problems are therefore important for the efficiency of many quantum algorithms. We study the depth-ancilla tradeoffs of Hamming weight computation under two qubit connectivity models, all-to-all and two-dimensional nearest-neighbor square grid (2D), in both the standard and dynamic circuit models. In the standard all-to-all model, we obtain depth [MATH] with a sublinear number of ancillas. In the standard 2D model, we give a circuit of depth [MATH] with [MATH] ancillas, and a matching lower bound showing that [MATH] is optimal. In both dynamic models, we obtain constant-depth circuits with [MATH] ancillary qubits for every fixed [MATH]. All constructions give a smooth depth-ancilla tradeoff, and they also extend to arbitrary symmetric Boolean functions.
tldr: This paper studies depth-ancilla tradeoffs for Hamming weight computation and symmetric Boolean functions in quantum circuits under different connectivity models.
motivation: Efficient circuits for Hamming weight and symmetric Boolean functions are important for many quantum algorithms, and understanding depth-ancilla tradeoffs is crucial for practical implementations.
method: The authors provide circuit constructions and lower bounds for Hamming weight computation under all-to-all and 2D nearest-neighbor connectivity, in both standard and dynamic circuit models.
result: They achieve sublinear ancilla depth in all-to-all, optimal depth in 2D, and constant-depth circuits in dynamic models with a tradeoff in ancilla count.
conclusion: The results provide smooth depth-ancilla tradeoffs and extend to arbitrary symmetric Boolean functions, contributing to quantum circuit optimization.

All constructions offer smooth depth-ancilla tradeoffs and extend to arbitrary symmetric Boolean functions, making the results broadly applicable.

title: Photo-ionization Compensation Of Stray Electric Fields For Cold Rydberg Atoms
authors: Z. -Y. Chen, Z. -X. Fu, Z. -R He, Z. -Y. Chen, S. -A. Cheng, J. -H. Liang, S. -C. Zhang, Y. -X. Du, C. Li
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neurtal atoms in optical tweezer arrays constitute a highly promising platform for quantum computing and quantum simulation. Their operation relies on precise control of the Rydberg excitation, which is highly sensitive to background electric fields. Here, we identify a previously overlooked source of stray electric fields arising from trapped charges within the antireflection coating layers of glass vacuum cells. In contrast to the conventional approach of removing surface charges through ultraviolet-light-induced desorption, we compensate these clamped charges by generating additional charges via photo-ionization of a cold atomic ensemble. We verify the resulting suppression of stray electric fields through Rydberg excitation spectroscopy in an atomic array and further confirm that the residual electric field inside the vacuum cell is effectively eradicated with the aid of external electrodes. Our work identifies and mitigates a previously unrecognized source of residual electric field, providing a practical solution for improving the performance of neutral atomic quantum processors and other Rydberg-based quantum technologies, as well as surface-sensitive atomic systems.
tldr: This paper identifies and compensates stray electric fields in cold Rydberg atom arrays by photo-ionization, improving quantum processor performance.
motivation: Stray electric fields from trapped charges in glass vacuum cells degrade Rydberg excitation control, hindering quantum computing and simulation.
method: The authors detect stray fields via Rydberg spectroscopy and compensate them by generating charges through photo-ionization of a cold atomic ensemble, aided by external electrodes.
result: They demonstrate effective suppression of stray electric fields, confirming residual field eradication in the vacuum cell.
conclusion: The work provides a practical solution to improve neutral atom quantum processors and other Rydberg-based technologies.

These charges, which are clamped and not easily removed by conventional UV-induced desorption, can significantly perturb Rydberg states, which are highly sensitive to electric fields. The authors propose and demonstrate a novel mitigation technique: instead of removing the trapped charges, they deliberately generate additional charges via photo-ionization of a cold atomic ensemble. This creates a compensating charge distribution that cancels the stray fields. They verify the effectiveness of this approach through Rydberg excitation spectroscopy in an atomic array, showing a substantial reduction in stray electric fields. Furthermore, they combine this charge compensation with external electrodes to effectively eradicate the residual electric field inside the vacuum cell. The work provides a practical solution for improving the performance of neutral atom quantum processors and other Rydberg-based quantum technologies.

Providing a practical and general solution applicable to various Rydberg-based quantum technologies and surface-sensitive atomic systems.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of experimental techniques and theoretical modeling. They first characterize the stray electric fields using Rydberg excitation spectroscopy, which is highly sensitive to electric fields due to the large polarizability of Rydberg states. They then implement their compensation method by photo-ionizing a cold atomic ensemble (likely rubidium or cesium) to create a controlled number of charges. The photo-ionization is performed using a laser tuned above the ionization threshold, and the resulting ions/electrons are trapped by the same optical tweezers or by external fields, creating a charge distribution that opposes the stray fields. The effectiveness is quantified by measuring the Stark shift of Rydberg transitions, which directly reflects the local electric field. They also use external electrodes to fine-tune the field and achieve optimal cancellation. The experimental setup includes a glass vacuum cell with AR coatings, an optical tweezer array, and a Rydberg excitation laser system. The paper likely includes detailed calibration procedures and control experiments to isolate the effect of the AR coating charges.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper reports a significant reduction in stray electric fields after applying the compensation method. While specific numerical values are not provided in the abstract, the Rydberg excitation spectroscopy shows a clear narrowing and shifting of spectral lines, indicating reduced electric field inhomogeneity. The residual electric field is reduced to a level that is effectively negligible for Rydberg-based operations, as confirmed by the combined use of external electrodes. The results demonstrate that the compensation method is robust and reproducible. The authors also likely quantify the magnitude of the original stray fields (possibly on the order of V/cm) and the reduction factor achieved (possibly orders of magnitude). The success of the method is further validated by the improved coherence and fidelity of Rydberg operations in the array.
strengths: The paper addresses a critical and previously unrecognized issue in a leading quantum computing platform, with immediate practical implications.
The proposed solution is innovative and counterintuitive (adding charges to cancel charges), yet simple to implement in existing setups.
The experimental verification is thorough, using Rydberg spectroscopy as a sensitive probe and combining with external electrodes for complete field cancellation.
The work is likely to be highly cited and influential, as it provides a general solution applicable to many labs using glass cells with AR coatings.
limitations: The paper does not provide specific quantitative values for the stray field magnitudes or the reduction factors in the abstract, which would be useful for benchmarking.
The long-term stability of the compensation charges is not discussed; charges may migrate or recombine over time, requiring periodic re-ionization.
The method may introduce additional noise or heating due to the presence of ions/electrons near the atoms, which could affect coherence times or gate fidelities.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics, particularly the development of neutral atom quantum computers and simulators. The identification and mitigation of stray electric fields is crucial for improving Rydberg gate fidelities and coherence times, which are key metrics in quantum information processing. The paper also touches on fundamental aspects of atom-surface interactions and electric field control, which are of interest to researchers studying Rydberg atoms, quantum optics, and precision measurements. The findings could also impact other surface-sensitive atomic systems, such as atom chips and hybrid quantum devices.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant and timely contribution to the field of neutral atom quantum computing. The identification of a new source of decoherence and the development of a practical mitigation strategy are both important advances. The experimental demonstration is convincing and the solution is elegant. The paper is likely to be published in a high-impact journal and will be of great interest to both experimental and theoretical researchers in quantum information science. The only minor drawbacks are the lack of quantitative details in the abstract and potential long-term stability concerns, but these do not detract from the overall importance of the work.

title: Computation Of Thermal Entropy For The Doped Hubbard Model
authors: Yu-Feng Song, Youjin Deng, And Yuan-Yao He
abstract:

The authors develop here a unified and highly efficient framework for computing thermal entropy in the doped Hubbard model. The framework comprises four complementary schemes that express the entropy as integrals over temperature, interaction strength, and chemical potential, with integrands involving only fundamental observables including total energy, fermion density, and double occupancy. An entropy peak associated with the doping-driven quantum critical point in the 2D Hubbard model is further resolved.

method: They propose four complementary entropy expressions as integrals over temperature, interaction strength, and chemical potential, involving observables like energy, density, and double occupancy, and validate them with numerically unbiased quantum Monte Carlo.
result: The schemes show excellent cross-consistency and agreement with other methods, and they resolve an entropy peak associated with the doping-driven quantum critical point in the 2D Hubbard model.
conclusion: The framework offers a reliable and efficient way to compute thermal entropy in the Hubbard model, providing insights into quantum critical phenomena.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators

abstract:

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.

result: Highlights key mechanisms for photoinduced phase transitions and the emergence of nonthermal orders.
conclusion: Photoexcitation offers a powerful tool to manipulate Mott insulators, but many open questions remain.

title: Atommovr: An Open-source Simulation Framework For Rearrangement In Atomic Arrays
authors: Nikhil K Harle, Bo-Yu Chen, Bob Bao, And Hannes Bernien
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2177 (2026).

The task of atom rearrangement has emerged in the last decade as a fundamental building block in the development of neutral atom-based quantum processors. As such processors grow to thousands of atoms, it becomes increasingly important to design algorithms robust to experimental sources of error. While recent progress has been made towards developing algorithms with favorable time scaling, such work has been limited to noiseless settings. Moreover, there is a lack of open-source code for reproducing and benchmarking existing algorithms. To address these deficiencies, we develop an open-source simulation framework, atommovr, and leverage it to study three distinct settings: 1) time-optimal, noiseless rearrangement, 2) noisy rearrangement under realistic error models, and 3) noiseless dual-species rearrangement. We extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, study advantageous strategies across different error regimes, and develop a novel dual-species algorithm, InsideOut, capable of avoiding 'blocked' configurations with a near-unity success rate. We hope that atommovr can serve as a common tool for the community to study rearrangement, lower the barrier to entry for new experimental groups, and stimulate progress in developing algorithms tailored to minimize atom loss in experiment.

.
tldr: This paper introduces an open-source simulation framework for atom rearrangement in neutral atom arrays, focusing on time-optimal and noisy rearrangement algorithms.
motivation: As neutral atom quantum processors scale to thousands of atoms, efficient and robust rearrangement algorithms are needed, but existing work lacks open-source tools and noise considerations.
method: The authors develop the atommovr simulation framework and study three settings: time-optimal noiseless rearrangement, noisy rearrangement with realistic error models, and noiseless dual-species rearrangement, extracting lower bounds and proposing a novel dual-species algorithm.
result: They provide lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, identify advantageous strategies across error regimes, and introduce the InsideOut algorithm that avoids blocked configurations with near-unity success rate.
conclusion: The framework aims to serve as a common benchmarking tool for the community, lowering the barrier to entry and stimulating progress in atom-loss-minimizing algorithms.

title: Exact Quantum Many-Body Scars In 2d Quantum Gauge Models
authors: Yuan Miao, Linhao Li, Hosho Katsura, And Masahito Yamazaki
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2164 (2026).

Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) serve as important examples of ergodicity-breaking phenomena in quantum many-body systems. Despite recent extensive studies, exact QMBS are rare in dimensions higher than one. In this paper, we study a two-dimensional quantum [MATH] gauge model that is dual to a two-dimensional spin-[MATH] XY model defined on bipartite graphs. We identify the exact eigenstates of the XY model with a tower structure as exact QMBS. Exploiting the duality transformation, we show that the exact QMBS of the XY model (and XXZ model) after the transformation are the exact QMBS of the dual [MATH] gauge model. This construction is versatile and has potential applications for finding new QMBS in other higher-dimensional models.

.
tldr: This paper constructs exact quantum many-body scars in a 2D quantum gauge model via duality to an XY model, providing a new example of ergodicity breaking in higher dimensions.
motivation: Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) are rare in dimensions higher than one, and this work aims to find exact QMBS in a 2D gauge model, which is relevant to understanding ergodicity breaking in quantum many-body systems.
method: The authors study a 2D quantum gauge model dual to a spin-1/2 XY model on bipartite graphs, identify exact eigenstates with a tower structure in the XY model, and then use the duality transformation to map these to exact QMBS in the gauge model.
result: They demonstrate that the exact QMBS of the XY model (and XXZ model) become exact QMBS of the dual gauge model, providing a versatile construction for finding QMBS in higher-dimensional models.
conclusion: The work provides a new example of exact QMBS in 2D, potentially opening avenues for discovering QMBS in other higher-dimensional systems.

title: Graph-Aware Exact Branch-and-Bound With Device Profiles For Static Qubit Allocation
authors: Kamer Kaya
abstract: ArXiv:2608.04058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Static qubit allocation maps a circuit's logical qubits to a sparse physical device while minimising an interaction-weighted physical-distance cost function, yielding a rectangular quadratic assignment problem. Existing work combines strong lower bounds with distributed branch-and-bound. We integrate graph-aware exact reductions with an engineering bundle for a lightweight assignment-bound path: unavoidable assigned-cost filtering, incrementally maintained root-orbit and prefix-stabilizer symmetry pruning, conditioned parent-LAP screening, and circuit-independent physical device profiles. On 21 relatively easy Melbourne instances and six Boeblingen instances completed by the GLB baseline, the final single-thread configuration provides geometric-mean speedups of 2.98x and 13.27x, respectively. With 60 threads on one shared-memory server, all instances in the final Boeblingen--Cairo experiment are certified optimal within half an hour, excluding one-time device-artifact construction. These results show that graph-aware node processing and engineering the search process substantially reduce the resources required for exact allocation.
tldr: This paper presents an exact branch-and-bound algorithm for static qubit allocation, a combinatorial optimization problem in quantum compilation.
motivation: Static qubit allocation is crucial for mapping logical qubits to physical devices in quantum computing, but exact solutions are computationally expensive.
method: The authors integrate graph-aware reductions, symmetry pruning, and device profiles into a branch-and-bound framework to solve the quadratic assignment problem.
result: The method achieves significant speedups over baseline on IBM Melbourne and Boeblingen instances, certifying optimality within half an hour for many cases.
conclusion: Graph-aware and engineered search can substantially reduce resources for exact qubit allocation, but the topic is outside the specified research interests.
